#18. 6 ways to make mornings smoother when your child has ADHD

Home / Health & Wellness / Children's Health

A child psychiatrist on the small systems that take the pressure off the hardest 20 minutes of the day.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 15, 2026

It’s 7:40, the bus comes at 7:52, and one shoe is missing. You’ve asked about the backpack four times. Your kid is half-dressed on the floor, watching dust move through a sunbeam.

If that’s your morning, you have company. About 1 in 9 US children, roughly 7.1 million kids, has been diagnosed with ADHD, according to CDC data. For a lot of those families, the hardest stretch of the day happens before anyone heads out the door.

There’s a reason mornings hit this hard, and it isn’t that your kid doesn’t care. Michael Morse, MD, a board-certified child and adolescent psychiatrist who directs the ADHD & Anxiety Center at Alvord Baker and is an associate professor of psychiatry at Georgetown University, says the morning routine requires a child “to do the most with the least help.” Many kids with ADHD run on a later internal clock, he says, so at 7 a.m. the brain regions that handle planning and time aren’t fully up and running, and yet, that’s when we ask kids to move through a string of boring steps against a deadline.

Executive function, the mental system for getting started, tracking time and shifting gears, tends to develop more slowly in kids with ADHD, so what looks like refusal is often a brain that can’t get itself going yet without help. “Kids do well when they can,” Morse says. For parents, that means making a mental shift from asking why your kid won’t do something to examining what’s getting in the way. That reframe can often help you resist a lecture and lend a hand instead. “Punishment can’t teach a skill a child doesn’t have yet,” he says, “but support can.”

“The best mornings usually start the evening before, when there’s time to think and nobody is racing the bus,” Morse says. Sign the permission slips, settle on what’s for breakfast, and, if your kid is old enough, have them pack their backpack and lay out clothes for the next day. (For younger kids, you’ll want to supervise this process.)

He also suggests a five-minute planning talk earlier in the day to look at what’s ahead for the day together, whether that’s gym, a test or a game after school, which helps a kid build their own sense of what’s coming.

Sleep is the biggest lever of all. “A tired brain makes every ADHD symptom worse,” Morse says, and it gets less benefit from medication. Sleep trouble is common here, affecting as many as half of kids with ADHD by some estimates. A steady bedtime, screens off about an hour before bed, and a warm bath or shower all make it easier for your child to nod off at night, which sets the stage for smoother mornings.

Kids with ADHD often can’t hold a string of instructions in mind, so “‘go get ready’ is really six instructions in three words,” Morse says. A visual sequence takes that load off their memory. In practice it’s a simple chart on the bathroom mirror listing each step in order: get dressed, eat breakfast, brush teeth, shoes on, backpack. Use pictures for younger kids and let them check off each step as they go, and build the chart together, since kids are more likely to follow a plan they helped make.

When your kid stalls, skip the fresh reminder and point back to the list with a quick “What’s next on your chart?” Do it long enough and “the chart becomes the reminder instead of the parent,” Morse says.

Many kids with ADHD experience time differently, something “called ‘time blindness,’ though some people prefer not to use that term,” Morse says. Either way, 10 minutes from now and an hour from now can feel about the same, so the tools that help are the ones that make time visible. A visual timer with a colored disk that shrinks as the minutes run out lets a kid see at a glance how much is left, and timers that announce the minutes work well for a kid dressing in another room.

Morse says “a simple timer that does one thing beats a phone,” since phones are designed to pull attention toward games and messages, the opposite of what a kid needs while getting ready.

Every choice in the morning is another chance to stall, and each stall may need an adult to jump-start things again. So take the decisions out ahead of time. Have your child select their outfit the night before or keep a few go-to options on rotation. “Some kids wear something close to a uniform and are relieved not to have to think about it,” Morse says. For breakfast, offer two pre-approved options, ideally with some protein like eggs or yogurt to keep energy steady throughout the day.

Give the backpack, shoes and jacket a single launch spot, one basket or hook where they always live, so nobody’s hunting a missing shoe at 7:40. The thread running through all of it, in Morse’s words, is “moving the thinking out of the morning and into the calm of the evening. Fewer decisions also mean fewer arguments.”

If your kid takes medication, when they take it can matter as much as whether they take it. “No ADHD medicine works the moment it’s swallowed,” Morse says, so a long-acting stimulant taken at breakfast may not kick in until a child is already at school, leaving the hardest part of the morning uncovered. Some families, with their doctor’s guidance, give the dose closer to wake-up so it has more time to start working, and some formulations are made to be taken the night before.

This one is a conversation for your prescriber rather than a change to make on your own. Timing is one factor that can impact a medication’s efficacy, so it’s worth raising at the next appointment.

“A few fixes come from love and still backfire,” Morse says. Dressing a dawdling second grader or racing a forgotten worksheet to school smooths the morning but teaches a kid they can’t manage on their own. Repeatedly raising your voice tends to pull everyone into a louder and louder standoff. And consequences rarely do the teaching, because “the problem was memory, not caring,” Morse says.

When a morning does come apart, the goal is to keep it from becoming a bad day between you and your kid. Once everyone’s out the door, the moment for teaching has passed, and a lecture in the car just sends a child into school ashamed and anxious. Try something simple instead, like “That was a rough morning. I love you, and we’ll figure it out.”

Later, when everyone’s calm, look at what broke together, since it’s usually one step you can fix without overhauling the whole routine. Go easy on yourself too. (And if you need a bit of support, Morse points parents to the work of psychologist Kristin Neff on self-compassion.)

None of this makes mornings frictionless. It hands the remembering to a system instead of to you, so you’re not the last thing standing between your kid and the 7:52 bus.

#21. Book-To-Screen Adaptations Coming In 2027 That Are Worth The Read First

If you just can’t wait to learn the endings... you don’t have to.

Lately it feels like we’re getting all kinds of exciting new casting announcements, from the two leads in the screen adaptation of Rebecca Yarros’ Fourth Wing to Florence Pugh fronting the movie adaptation of Matt Haig’s The Midnight Library. But for now, those projects have release dates of “TBD.” So what incredible books will we get to see play out on the big screen in the near future? Here are all the best book-to-screen adaptations coming in 2027, so you can read the book beforehand if that’s your jam.

Author Tomi Adeyemi’s rich storytelling will come alive just two weeks into the New Year, when her novel Children of Blood and Bone comes to theaters and IMAX. The film will star Thuso Mbedu as Zélie, Damson Idris, Amandla Stenberg, Regina King, Cynthia Erivo, Idris Elba, and the incredible Viola Davis, to name just a portion of the cast.

There are three books in Adeyemi’s Legends of Orïsha triology, all available now, if you want to read through to the end between now and mid-January.

If you have Apple TV, you’ll want to start Neuromancer when it drops on Jan. 22. Based on William Gibson’s sci-fi cyberpunk novel published in 1984, the 10-episode series will follow Case, a hacker-slash-hustler, and Molly, a cyborg mercenary, through a dangerous heist that will pit them against AI (timely), massive corporations, and all the powers-that-be.

Greta Gerwig’s take on Narnia is coming and it can’t get here soon enough, TBH. Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew is based on the 1955 novel The Magician’s Nephew by C.S. Lewis, the sixth published (but first in the timeline of the story) novel in the children’s series The Chronicles of Narnia.

This movie is getting a true theatrical release in February, then hitting Netflix to stream at home on April 2, 2027. Either way, we can’t wait to see Meryl Streep and Daniel Craig in these magical roles.

Feb. 12 is going to be a big day at the box offices. In Kristen Hannah’s novel by the same name, she captures the story of World War II from the perspective of two sisters, who will no doubt be played beautifully by actual sisters Dakota and Elle Fanning. Go into this theater armed with tissues, and read Hannah’s book now if you’d like to know why.

Spoiler alert! At the end of Season 1, Shane and Ilya’s relationship is revealed, setting up the central tension of Season 2. What will the fallout be, and how will the pair weather it together? All we’ll say is that apparently “intimacy rehearsals” are well underway...

While a more specific release date hasn’t been announced yet, if you’d like to read ahead, Season 2 of the show is based on The Long Game, which is Book 6 in author Rachel Reid’s Game Changers series.

A summer read turned summer blockbuster? We’re here for it. Starring Phoebe Dynevor and Patrick Schwarzenegger as January and Gus, we get to watch these two authors who have no business falling in love do exactly that. The rest of the cast seems stellar too: think Andie MacDowell, Kristin Davis, Tig Notaro, and Kevin Bacon.

The movie adaptation of this bestselling novel by Gabrielle Zevin stars Daisy Edgar-Jones as Sadie Green, Sky Yang as Sam Masur, and Sean Kaufman as Marx Watanabe. Childhood friends Sadie and Sam collaborate on a blockbuster video game, Ichigo, which launches the two undergrads to fame. What follows is a story than spans 30 years and follows the pair through all of life’s unexpected ups and downs.

We know that Bridgerton Season 5 is coming to Netflix in 2027, though a more exact date isn’t ours to know just yet. But if you’d like a preview of what’s to come, you can pick up Julia Quinn’s When He Was Wicked, the Bridgerton novel this season of the hit series will draw from.

#22. 12 Birthday Party Themes Kids Are *Really* Into Right Now

Birthday party trends come and go, but kids remain impressively committed to whatever they’ve decided is their entire personality (this month). The good news: 2026’s biggest kids’ birthday party ideas are less about matching every plate and napkin and more about giving kids something fun to actually *do*. Think KPop karaoke, bracelet bars, race tracks, baking stations, and plenty of ways to turn a favorite obsession into a party without building an elaborate balloon installation at midnight (we’ve literally all been there).

We only recommend what we’ve independently researched, selected, and genuinely love. If you purchase through our links, we may earn a commission (at no extra cost to you).

If your kid has spent the better part of the year singing “Golden” at full volume, this is one of the most popular kids’ birthday party ideas that probably doesn’t require much convincing. Turn the obsession into an easy party with karaoke, a dance-off, glow lights, and a few over-the-top accessories. A just-add-water, kid-friendly ramen bar makes feeding everyone easy. Bonus: a karaoke machine handles both the theme and the entertainment, which is exactly the kind of multitasking we support.

#24. Jefferson Fisher Has The Secret to Getting Along Better With Absolutely Everyone

The lawyer, author, and influencer wants us to talk more and argue less. He might just be onto something.

If being a parent, a husband, a man, a human has taught me anything at all it’s that communication is everything. Also, most of us suck at communication.

For once, our poor communication is not a product of big external forces — neither isolationist politics nor overcooked capitalism nor a failing of modern masculinity. We can only blame ourselves because, hey, communicating is hard. Getting your point across to a group, your nuclear family, or one single person takes practice and discipline, mistakes and learning. I don’t think we ever get it entirely right.

Well, most of us don’t. There are some communicators in this world that are … blessed. Jefferson Fisher is one such individual. Fisher is a Texan, dad, husband, and personal injury attorney who has made a name for himself through social videos that teach us all how to communicate better.

The videos offer pithy lessons like this: Instead of saying I disagree, “tweak it a little and say, I see things differently.” Why? “When you talk in terms of perspective, you find more connection.” Here’s another: “How I talk to my kids will affect how they talk to their kids.”

Simple, pointed, and poignant. You can see why millions tune in.

Fisher’s goal is to make people talk more and argue less. It says just that on the cover of his fantastic, practical, wonderfully written book The Next Conversation — a must read for all of us who strive to get along a little better with those around us.

We caught up with Fisher to talk about his new book and, naturally, anoint him as the latest Cool Dad. Here are some excerpts from our talk, including extras from the Cool Dad Questionnaire and his advice for the most important conversations you’ll ever have.

What’s one thing you wish your kids had today from your childhood?

Probably more of a reckless abandon about what they ate. I grew up in just every Little Debbie from Cosmic Brownies to ... everything you could think of that was probably terrible for us, but we didn't know any different.

I mean, this is my guess ... I would say what Sierra loves about me is my steadiness. When things don't go to plan, I'm pretty rock steady. So when there is something unexpected or the kids go into what we call their midnight madness, when it's right there at bedtime and they're absolutely losing their minds, that's when I'm able to step in and I think I'm able to really notice when she's overwhelmed, and take over.

And what do you think they maybe find annoying about you?

I mean, there's lots. I'm trying to find a really good one like she finds the most annoying about me is sometimes I can be a little bit occasionally of like a party-pooper where the kids are just ... all going nuts and I'm like, "Can we just not yell so much in our house?" So there's that.

Probably the bigger thing she gets more annoyed about is my relationship with money. Its just money. So I'm the spender and so she is the saver. If it's something that's like, "Hey, but this would be fun, even though it's not something we exactly need right now, but it would be a cool memory," I think there's a lot of that.

What does fatherhood mean to you in our current world?

Fatherhood, with the caveat of doing it well to be a good father, I think, is knowing it's a discipline and not a destination. It's a daily devotion to putting your wife, your spouse, your partner, your kids before you. And it's this idea of ... are you inconveniencing them for your comfort or is it the opposite, are you willing to inconvenience yourself for their comfort?

There are times where it's going to be uncomfortable. I don't want to be the one carrying all the bags all the time, but is it what my family needs in that moment in the airport? Yeah, that's what they need. Can I do it? Yeah.

I got to say that the carrying bags all the time is a wonderful metaphor.

Yeah. You're the one that is supposed to shoulder the heavy. So you're supposed to carry what they can't. I'm sure there's a similarity to this phrase of to be what others cannot, you must be willing to suffer what others will not, and so it's like that. To be the dad that others can't, you got to be able to do what others won't.

How do you better communicate with your partner in parenting? Do you think there's ways that you, something that don't apply, or do you follow the advice in your book and have great arguments and conversations with your spouse?

I wouldn't say there are things that don't apply. I would say what it would need to go deeper on is the theme of repair specifically. So you could have the mindset of arguments and that's something that's very helpful. There's the idea of saying things with control, meaning be regulated and knowing when you need to take that timeout, and using the pauses. But the turn the book doesn't make with regard to marital relationships is repair.

We are talking about words of affirmation, affirming somebody's feelings, being able to take ownership of your words and what that actually sounds like ... how to truly use words of empathy and affirm how they feel, how to say things that are going to bring. We hit on connection in the book, but more in the way of framing non-relationship conversations.

In repair, there is a lot of something as simple as, "Yes, I said that. Yes, I did that. I absolutely can see how that would have frustrated you or upset you," or "I think it's totally reasonable for you to feel this way. I don't blame you for being upset about that. I could have done that better." And then how to actually, words of apology, how to repair after a rupture, that to me is, that's a whole different ballgame, whole different set of skills.

What do you think about checking in? I'm wondering where that falls in the communication line. It's maybe a little bit of the repair, but is that an important thing to do or how do you feel about just what a felt of unspoken understanding between family?

There's an element that my wife and I do and that's check-ins and check-outs. I mean, it's what we call them, things that we do in the morning and things that we do in the evening. Otherwise, there are times you may never talk to your spouse in the day and you know what that's like. Before you know it, you're just two people, somehow there's a woman who lives with me. I don't know who she is, but she's here and you can be roommates that way if you're not checking in with each other. The other is that unspokenness of knowing when something is wrong and that you feel like you might be approaching things from a different vantage. I like asking the phrase, "What's coming up?" "What's coming up for you?"

Instead of me saying, "What's wrong with you" or even, "What's up with you?" That tends to get a pretty defensive response. But if I say something as simple as what's coming up, there's a difference between [that and] saying, "How are you and how's your heart?"

#26. 11 Leftover Turkey Recipes That Aren't Just Sandwiches

Thanksgiving may be over but you still wanna eat good.

I love Thanksgiving and look forward to it all year, not only because it’s a wonderful day with family, but because I get to eat so many of my favorite foods in one meal. And perhaps the best part of all is that there are often so many leftovers, I don’t have to cook again for a good long while (hallelujah!). That said, even the biggest Turkey Day feast fans get tired of leftovers by Day 3. As the days wear on, you’ll want to have some leftover turkey recipes that aren’t just sandwiches in your arsenal. Chances are you got tired of those on Day 2.

Take your turkey, mashed potatoes, gravy, stuffing, and cranberry sauce up in some crescent roll dough and bake — that’s Budget Bytes’ idea to use up your leftovers. Add your remaining gravy to the center, cut, and dunk!

Pretty much any food combo that’s already yummy somehow tastes even better as an egg roll. Dinners Done Quick’s recipe will teach you how to turn turkey and your favorite sides into a delicious, golden appetizer the next day.

Stuffing, turkey, a little bit of spinach, and plenty of eggs will get you these delicious stuffing muffins, courtesy of Budget Bytes. They’re an easy on-the-go breakfast or quickly reheatable lunch that’s reminiscent of Thanksgiving, but different enough to feel new.

Chicken salad fans, guess what? You can just sub in turkey instead of chicken to make your favorite wraps and sammies. All The Healthy Things’ recipe is herby and crunchy thanks to all the fresh dill, celery, diced red onions, and those leftover pecans from that pie you baked.

Simply LaKita is an expert at comfort food recipes, so I trust her leftover turkey and rice soup is every bit as smoky, cozy, and hug-in-a-bowl-worthy as she describes. Serve it with the remaining rolls and butter from dinner and no one will be disappointed.

Thanksgiving food is so good because it’s nostalgic and comforting. If you want to keep that feeling going, turning your leftovers into a turkey pot pie à la Princess Pinky Girl’s recipe is perfect. What could be better on a cold evening with a cozy new Christmas movie cued up?

I would never think to put my Thanksgiving leftovers on top of potato skins, but Budget Bytes is just a genius like that. You might have a few little potatoes left over from mashing all their friends. This recipe will help you turn them into a yummy appetizer for football Sunday, topped with turkey remnants, cranberries, stuffing, and cheese.

Here, Dinners Done Quick’s recipe reminds us that you can honestly make sheet pan nachos out of anything, including your leftover turkey, cranberries, and corn. With a few extra fixings, like pickled onions and banana peppers, they’ll taste like a totally fresh dish.

Again, cooked turkey can be subbed into pretty much any recipe that normally calls for chicken. Damn Delicious’ turkey enchiladas are proof. They’ll help you empty your fridge of all that white meat, and if you’re someone who thinks turkey leans too dry, enchilada sauce and cheese will take care of that for you.

Princess Pinky Girl’s leftover turkey casserole only takes 10 minutes to prep and 40 minutes in the oven. It serves six as written, but would be easy enough to double if you have enough turkey to use up and your (hungry) guests are still in town.

Sliders are technically a sandwich, sure, but these are not two simple pieces of white bread with turkey and cranberry sauce in between. No, Damn Delicious’ sliders are oven-baked little morsels layered with turkey, cranberry relish, and cheese, but you could absolutely add your favorite sides on top too.

I can feel the tryptophan kicking in already! Who’s ready for Thanksgiving leftovers and a nap?

#27. To make mom friends, I rediscovered my religion

Having a hard time connecting with other moms? My advice: Head to your favorite house of worship.

By Hannah Pasternak Updated Oct. 15, 2026

A woman, in her life, will make several types of friends. Childhood friends, camp friends, college friends, work friends, and, for those who opt in during the reproductive years, mom friends. The lattermost of these always seemed like an endpoint to me—the hardest level in a game I’ve spent three decades playing. A rite of passage that marks the final frontier of girlhood.

Finding your people in motherhood is difficult. Until your child is in school, you are left floating through fix-ups with friends of friends and families you meet at the playground. Daycare can feel transient, and making solid friends at the small in-home program my daughter attends took more than a year.

You may, like me, have pre-existing close friends who have kids around the same time as you, but they may not live in your neighborhood, let alone your state, and therefore are categorized in their primary, or original, friendship bucket.

Mom friends are unique, made and dependent upon another relationship—that of your child and their child, and what they have in common—and time-dependent, too. Can you meet up on a whim? Would they like to grab that post-drop-off coffee? (This, I’m convinced, is not really something that exists in real life, only in the 90s and on television.) Is it ever really that easy?

Perhaps you have had better luck than me, but the only way I’ve managed to make mom friends is by relying on the oldest trick from, well, the oldest book: religion.

Nearly every Saturday morning, my husband and I  take our daughter to our synagogue at 10 a.m for “Tot Shabbat,” as it’s commonly called. It is just two blocks from our apartment, in a century-old building with magnificent stained glass windows and a ceiling that may be caving in. I take my daughter to a multipurpose room with basketball court floors while the main Sabbath prayer service goes on in the sanctuary. The kids, ages five and below, play together on a blue carpet, with blocks and Magnatiles and cars.

The moms and dads drink our coffees and schmooze. After a while, we do Circle Time, where a wonderful twentysomething teacher leads the kids in songs about gratitude and spiritual tradition. Pom-poms are involved. We are usually there until noon. Oh, and none of us have our phones. And that is how I finally made mom friends.

I realize this makes me an outlier. In a 2023 column for the New York Times, Jessica Grose described the decrease in church attendance as perhaps the “largest and fastest religious shift in America.” The following year, Grose wrote again about young women in particular fleeing organized religion in droves, largely in response to traditional ideologies around bodily autonomy and gender roles. A 2025 study showed that more than one in four Americans consider themselves unaffiliated with organized religion. I can tell you that many people bristle when I share that we observe the weekly Jewish Sabbath, assuming it’s restrictive and overly conservative or anachronistic. Culturally, amongst moms my age who live in urban centers, it just doesn’t seem to be en vogue.

When organized religion is embraced, it’s often by Gen Z, who are curious about its benefits—community, ritual, connection, belief—in an otherwise isolating time. The Wall Street Journal recently claimed that New York City’s newest hotspot is Sunday Mass. Last year, the New York Times wrote about the resurgence of the cross necklace amongst White House staffers and pop stars alike. Elle covered the cross-as-jewelry-trend even earlier, in 2024. As far as modern takes on traditional Judaism go, a hospitality concept called Shtick, founded by producer Jacqueline Lobel, creates editorial Friday night dinners and other parties that celebrate “the quintessential Jewish foods and customs found here in New York City.” In 2025, one such event included a Shabbat dinner for the Council of Fashion Designers of America.

So perhaps there is something to be said about what turning inside yourself, or to your family and its denominational history, can offer. Perhaps there is something to be said about the foundation that a shared belief or tradition can provide. A place of worship, if you find the right one, is also a place that naturally builds local community. (A mommy and me class there can, for what it’s worth, also cost less than a trip to the children’s museum.)

When I started bringing my daughter to our synagogue, it was more of a survival strategy than anything else. She was just six months old, a poor napper and always happier when we were out of the house. She could barely sit up, let alone play with other kids. The other mothers seemed seasoned and poised like veterans, worlds ahead of who I was and what I knew about raising a child. I mostly kept to myself and tried to listen in to everyone else’s conversations. Some moms were nice, asking me my name and gawking at my baby. I kept on showing up.

After my daughter turned one, there was a great shift. A new wave of babies joined the group, all learning to walk and eat chicken and extend their attention spans. This would be her “class,” a group of girls all born within the same six-month period who had finally dropped their morning nap (“What morning nap?” my daughter, if she could talk then, would have said) and were ready to build towers and clap during Circle Time.

Together, my daughter and I hit our groove. Soon we started to get invited for Shabbat lunch at her new friends’ homes, and we invited them to ours. As the mothers stuff the children into their coats and wipe kugel off their faces, we agree to meet again in Central Park later in the day. And because it is Shabbat, and none of us use our phones for 25 hours, we simply fly by the seat of our pants and commit to our plans and show up. When we get to the park we talk to each other, because no one is working or texting or scrolling. It’s very bucolic, and yet it feels like an alternate reality every single Saturday, orbiting the rest of my social life.

So this is the scene of my “mom friends.” We all live in the same neighborhood, but do different things for work. Many of us didn’t know each other before mommy and me, and we all have lives and friends of our own, outside of our motherhood. Our WhatsApp chat errs on the side of purely logistical, confirming our weekly meetup or a sporadic special event—a Purim puppet show, a Hanukkah celebration.

I think this is what religion, as divisive as it can be, is meant to bring to our lives. A place to go with your kid every Saturday morning, the will to keep showing up, people who expect you to be there. And if you’re lucky, kugel.

#29. Top Terrarium Kits for Kids: Fun, Creative, and Educational

Gone are the days of arts and crafts sets that simply involve painting a range of suncatchers to hang up in the window or arranging a fall wreath using pieces of foam leaves because the art of the terrarium kit has fully caught steam this year! Terrarium kits are an engaging way for your kid to experience an easily digestible dose of science mixed with using their own sense of creativity in an activity that doesn't involve a ton of fuss or mess.

The really cool thing about terrarium kits for kids is that there's plenty of variety that can appeal to your child's other interests. For instance, if you have a kid who just loves the idea of cultivating green life on their own, there are ones geared towards creating a cozy den for your seedlings and adding some decorative items for a bit of interest. If your child has always loved heading to your local Natural History Museum to spend a few hours browsing all the dinosaur exhibits, there are terrarium kits that integrate making a miniature dinosaur habitat. To find the coolest terrarium kit for your kid that's going to get them excited, keep reading!

Get ready to inspire the next generation of innovators with these must-have STEM gifts!

According to PBS.org, a terrarium is a "micro-environment" where moisture typically evaporates, condensates, and can fall back down similar to rain, in an enclosed glass container. Every terrarium kit for kids will come with different guidelines depending on the theme and what it has to offer, as there are some terrarium kits for kids that are more geared towards engaging in their artistic sense and giving kids the tools to build their own micro-ecosystem with things like rainbow sand, colored pebbles, moss, and miniature unicorns. It really depends on your child's tastes, abilities, and what gets them excited when it comes to this hands-on activity, because there really is a terrarium kit out there for everyone.

Science experiment kits often contain plenty of items to perform over ten or more experiments. Here are the best science experiment kits for kids.

For some parents, it can feel difficult to gauge what science or craft kit is going to be right for them because there's an abundance of choice. If you need a little help trying to decide on the best terrarium kit for your child, here are a few pointers.

Whenever you're considering a STEM-related kit or an arts and craft activity for your children, it's always best to check out the suggested manufacturer's age because they've worked out what should be an age-appropriate activity for kids based on their skill set and abilities. You always want to be sure that your kid is getting hands-on with an activity that's safe and doesn't include any materials or parts that may pose a problem for their safety.

One of the hardest parts when it comes to terrarium kits for kids is picking out the right one for your child, which hopefully causes a few squeals of delight when they open it. It's always a good idea to think about their interests and passions and move forward from there. For instance, if your kid isn't that interested in growing things but will likely appreciate the artistic aspect of their own terrarium, you may want to opt for a mermaid or unicorn-themed terrarium that's brightly colored and full of opportunities to use their imagination.

Once they're done, if they want to place their magical creation on their bedside table and use it as a nightlight, they can turn on the LED light and even change the colors each night with the included remote control.

#30. 300 Beautiful Muslim Baby Names And Their Meanings

150 boy names and 150 girl names, filled with history, beauty, and qualities a child can grow into.

Choosing a baby name can begin with sound, family tradition, or a meaning that catches you at exactly the right moment. Some names feel strong and grounded; others bring to mind light, tenderness, wisdom, or the beauty of the natural world. Then there are the ones that simply sound right when spoken aloud.

Muslim baby names draw from a rich range of languages, histories, and naming traditions. Arabic and Quranic choices appear here alongside other names found within Muslim families and communities. Some are familiar favorites, while others may offer something less commonly heard.

Meanings and English spellings can vary between languages, regions, and transliteration styles, so it is worth checking the pronunciation and cultural context before making a final choice. Ahead, find 300 Muslim baby names and the meanings connected to them.

Ihsan – Excellence; kindness; beautiful conduct

Tahsin – Improvement; enrichment; beautification

Delara – Beloved; one who delights the heart

Layan – Softness; gentleness; comfortable living

Rayhana – Fragrant basil; sweet-scented plant

A beautiful meaning is an important beginning, but a name also lives through pronunciation, family history, and the culture in which a child will grow. Say your favorites with the family name, write them down, and ask relatives how they sound in the languages your child may hear at home.

Often, the right choice is the one that feels natural when spoken and holds something your family hopes to pass on. It may be waiting somewhere in this list, or one name may lead you back to a family favorite you had not considered before. Either way, that moment of recognition is worth waiting for.

#33. 33 Incredible Thanksgiving Desserts (That Aren’t Pie)

From pumpkin rolls to cranberry crisp, there are so many more ways to bring fall flavors to your spread (Hello, no-churn ice cream!). For anyone craving Thanksgiving desserts that aren’t pie, we have Turkey Day recipe inspiration to offer that includes gluten-free and vegan recipes for the folks in your life with special dietary needs.

For a festive flavor that goes beyond the usual apple or pumpkin pie, spice up your Thanksgiving dessert with a bit of ginger. This decadent Chinese five-spice cake from The Cozy Apron, topped with ginger buttercream and candied ginger, will invigorate your taste buds after all of that turkey.

If you’re looking for an easy Thanksgiving dessert that isn’t pie, these pumpkin mini muffins from Averie Cooks are coated with sugar and cinnamon and packed with fall flavor. Actually, you don’t need to wait until dessert—they can be a sweet way to start your Thanksgiving morning! And they’re vegan.

Related: 10 Vegetarian Mains You Can Serve for Thanksgiving

For a decadent Thanksgiving dessert that isn’t pie, put a twist on the classic cheesecake flavor profile with this winner of a recipe from Sweet Peas and Saffron. It’s totally adaptable to your taste preferences when it comes to cranberry sauce, and the individual portions make serving a breeze.

Use a winter fruit that doesn’t get a lot of love for your Thanksgiving dessert this year with this recipe from Boulder Locavore that isn’t pie. It’s got warming spices like ginger, cinnamon, and allspice, and is covered in a sweet glaze.

Okay, so there’s nothing about banana pudding that screams “fall,” but it’s one of those desserts that’s hard to pass on. Live Well Bake Often has a great recipe for this classic sweet treat.

You can whip up this Pumpkin Roll from Tastes Better from Scratch, and then freeze it before the big day. Canned pumpkin and cream cheese are just two of the delightful ingredients that come together in this dessert that’s both creative and cute. Your treat will be the talk of the Thanksgiving dinner table!

Take inspiration from Mangia Bedda, and whip up a pretty apple cake for your holiday table. The addition of yogurt makes the cake extra moist, and if the whole thing isn’t gobbled up on Thanksgiving, it’ll taste great the next morning with a cup of coffee.

Make sure there’s something for everyone on your dessert table with these gluten-free cupcakes from A Table Full of Joy. Topped with a brown sugar buttercream, they’re bound to be a hit with your whole crew.

Keep it simple this Thanksgiving by making A Simple Palate’s tried-and-true apple crumble. It’s much quicker than making a pie, but it tastes just as good—especially when paired with a scoop of vanilla ice cream.

If you’ve got chocolate fans in your family, they’ll definitely fall in love with these fudgy brownies from Averie Cooks. They’re super quick to make and are topped with a yummy layer of pumpkin and chocolate chips.

How cute are these pumpkin bars from Oh My Goodness Chocolate Desserts? We love the criss-cross pattern of cream cheese on top, and we’re happy to report that they taste as good as they look.

We’ve fallen in love with these cranberry shortbread bars from Easy Wholesome, and we’re pretty sure you’ll feel the same way, too. Rich and tender shortbread pairs beautifully with the tart cranberry filling, and a crumble topping finishes it off.

The vegans in your crew don’t need to miss out on dessert, thanks to Coley Cooks. With the help of cashews, dates, and coconut milk, it’s surprisingly easy to make this vegan pumpkin cheesecake.

Did somebody say Nutella? The Savvy Kitchen combines the sweet goodness of Nutella with the traditional spice of pumpkin for a cake that looks as good as it tastes.

If you need to consider certain dietary restrictions at your Thanksgiving meal—but still want the wow factor when it comes to dessert—this spicy but sweet cake from Fragrant Vanilla Cake might just be the answer.

If you have a box of brownie mix, then you're halfway to making this sweet turkey tart, courtesy of The First Year. The most important ingredient is M&Ms for decorating—and since you only need a few select colors, we won't tell if you snack on the blues and greens.

Erin Clarke of Well Plated created a simpler version of the classic tarte tatin that's easy to make, absolutely delicious, and looks beautiful too. Get the recipe here.

Who can resist a scoop of ice cream, especially when it's bursting with fall flavors? This homemade version from The View from Great Island includes five different spices and pumpkin puree. Best of all, you don't need an ice cream maker!

The oven is already going to be working overtime on Thanksgiving Day, so why not take advantage of these creamy, no-bake parfaits from The Cozy Apron? If you're worried about your fancy stemware, serve the kids' desserts in plastic cups. Either way, your guests will be impressed by your creative Thanksgiving dessert that isn't pie.

Can't decide between pumpkin pie and pecan pie? There's no need, thanks to this dessert from Glorious Treats that combines the two. This treat is made for jars, which is perfect for saving or giving as gifts, too.

Related: 12 Pumpkin Pie Recipes to Cap Off Your Thanksgiving Feast

Apple crisp is one of our favorite fall desserts, and this easy recipe from Plated Cravings is bound to be a Turkey Day win. It’s super quick to make and tastes amazing paired with whipped cream or ice cream.

For a super quick but impressive dessert, you’ve got to try this cake from Averie Cooks. With a boxed cake mix as its base, it comes together in no time and makes for a guaranteed crowd-pleaser.

This pumpkin crisp from Sara at Bitz & Giggles is not only delicious—it's also super simple to make. You probably already have the ingredients you need! Make it à la mode for an extra special Thanksgiving dessert that isn't pie.

Maybe you have so much on your plate cooking the big meal that the idea of adding dessert to your to-do list is a tad too much. That's where Chelsea's Messy Apron comes in. These treats are not only no-bake, but they're also really creative. Recruit the kids to help, and you have dessert and activities crossed off with one "recipe."

#34. My 5 Year Old Can’t Stop Saying F*ck

God love her ‘cause she uses it correctly, too.

My five year old won’t stop saying fuck. And before anyone suggests I investigate where she learned it, lemme save you the time.

Both my husband and I swear a lot. More than we should, probably. And definitely more than we should around someone who is still learning to write her name. We need to reel it in, and I know it. Unfortunately, knowing it and remembering to do it in the moment are two different things.

And we have backup. As the youngest of four, with a 13-year-old at the top, all her siblings swear too. There is no shortage of material. Add in all the stuff the older kids are watching on TV and my youngest is basically getting a PhD in inappropriate language.

And God love her because she uses it correctly. She understands placement and timing. She nails emphasis when she knows the moment calls for something a little extra. She isn’t just saying a forbidden word to get a response from us, she is actually making a point. And a lot of times, she nails it.

And because of that it can be very hard to parent her with a straight face. I mean, I know I need to be the adult in the room. I know laughing doesn’t help. But when a little girl in pigtails throws out a perfectly timed “f*#%”, it just kills me. I think it’s funny, and I respect the skill. But, I also need it to stop.

And it’s pretty hard to sell her on the seriousness of a rule when the rest of the house is operating under a different one. We are telling her she can’t say a word that the rest of use – well — a lot. But, she’s now in kindergarten. She’s in a classroom with a teacher and a lot of little kids who don’t have older siblings or trash-mouthed parents and for that reason, we needed to get it under control.

So, my husband and I landed on a threat: If she kept swearing, we were going to tell her teacher.

Yes, our big, scary, mature parenting strategy was to find another adult to deal with it. Whatever.

But we thought it would work. She seemed to understand when we told her, and seemed a little nervous about the possibility — enough, maybe, to work.

But then I picked her up from school last Friday. She hopped in the car and happily announced, “Well, Mom, I told Miss Williamson that I drop F-bombs. So, now you don’t have to!”

Apparently she considered the situation and took it upon herself to get ahead of it.

So while we do still need to reel it in at home and set a better example, at least telling Miss Williamson is off my to-do list.

And honestly, my kid is a fucking legend.

Samm is an ex-lawyer and mom of four who swears a lot. Find her on Instagram @sammbdavidson.

#35. ‘Elder Millennial’ comedian Iliza Shlesinger convinced her kids ‘from the window to the wall’ is about a nap party

The comedian on raising two little kids, the help she refuses to hide, and what being an elder Millennial mom really means.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 13, 2026

Iliza Shlesinger’s kids are allowed to watch cartoons, but nothing too grown-up. At the same time, they occasionally hear whatever’s thumping through the wall of her home office, where she’s been teaching herself to DJ. “It’s a lot of songs about female anatomy, and a lot of words we don’t use in real life,” she says.

She tries to turn it down, but doesn’t turn it off. The playlist is the exact stuff elder millennials have been getting down to since high school and college, and like many of us, she fully embraces the anthems. “These are the songs of my people,” she says. “This is called ‘Salt Shaker.’ We’re gonna go from the window to the wall, and I will tell you it’s about a nap party.”

As a fellow elder millennial myself, this jarring contrast is quite familiar. We dropped it low in the club once. Just because we’re hauling kids from school to soccer practice now, are we supposed to forget how to back that ass up?

Shlesinger, 43, has spent close to two decades turning this self-awareness into stand-up. Her 2018 Netflix hour “Elder Millennial” gave us the phrase to define a very specific subset of a generation. She’s still at it, with her latest special, “A Different Animal,” and the ongoing ILIZA! LIVE tour. On her podcast “Ask Iliza Anything,” she hands out blunt advice to strangers like the no-filter friend you trust with your most-unhinged questions. There’s a new Pampers campaign too. And there’s her home, shared with her husband, chef Noah Galuten, 4-year-old daughter and a 2-year-old son.

We got the exclusive chance to ask Shlesinger about what it means to parent as an elder millennial and how it feels to learn at 43 that Pampers wipes were never supposed to come out six at a time.

It’s no secret that motherhood requires a deep, personal shift. That doesn’t make it less difficult to navigate. You’re still the same person under there, the one who knows every word to “Salt Shaker,” and at the same time you’re turning into someone new you’re still getting to know. And though her kids aren’t newborns, the evolution continues to catch her off guard.

“I’m shocked at how often I’m re-realizing what a mom I am,” she says. Everything from the way she puts her jeans on to the fact that somehow, her phone flashlight is always on. “This didn’t happen like, five years ago. I was cool,” she offered with a declarative tone any elder millennial can relate to. Similarly, she recently snapped a naked selfie for her husband and clocked the kids’ toys in the shot. “Yes, they’re his kids, and it’s our bathroom. But that’s not hot.”

Part of parenting as a millennial is the urge to give your kids the childhood you had, or the best of it anyway, and the slow realization that you really can’t. The world they’re growing up in doesn’t match the one that made you. Shlesinger ran into that gap with a thought about her daughter. “She’s not going to go to my school and have my memories,” she says. “Once I internalized that, I got goosebumps. It’s up to me to make it just as nice as possible.” She can’t transfer the memories, so she’s salvaging the ingredients, keeping what worked and leaving the rest. “Picking all the good stuff from growing up. A scary story, a fun tradition. Letting go if it doesn’t work.”

In the name of creating new traditions, she’s gone all out with fall decor in the form of an elaborate front-yard autumn tableau, lifted straight from her Texas childhood. “I always saw the houses that decorated for fall as the ones that felt comfortable and safe, and the world feels so unsafe now,” she says. What that produced is an epic scene of controlled insanity. “So I’ve become that Texas mom. I paid cash for men to deliver bales of hay and oversized pumpkins that are rotting in the heat right now. No one on my block did it. None of my friends did it. My husband did not care.”

The display is firmly autumnal, not a drop of fake blood or oversize cobweb in sight, which is precisely why her 4-year-old objects. Her daughter wants spiders and gore, but she’s getting hay bales and tasteful gourds. “I’m like, we’re not doing that. It’s autumn.“

When asked how she manages parenting two kids alongside a bustling career, Shlesinger gives the answer few are willing to admit. “Do you want the honest answer that no one’s allowed to give, because people will say you’re unrelatable? I have a nanny. I’ve always had a nanny. We have help.”

Shlesinger believes that women are meant to raise kids in the company of other women. “It’s about letting other women help you parent. Letting other personality types in. Learning from other women.”

In fact, she didn’t crack a single manual. “I didn’t read one parenting book. I work, I have a career. I figured I’d wing it.” And she defers to her hired caregiver without ego. “Anything she said, I just did. I did not hire her to argue with her.”

She’s also clear that other women should have the same support. “If we lived in a country that valued women and parenting, and put money toward giving mothers resources so they can afford childcare, I wouldn’t have to tell you I pay for a nanny,” she says. “Other countries, the village raises them. We decided to make it very hard, for deeply misogynistic reasons, to let women be fully realized artistically and career-wise, and be mothers [at the same time].”

Like most of us, Iliza admits she’s learning as she goes. Take, for example, baby wipes. Every parent knows how hard it is to pull out just one wipe while one hand remains committed to a squirming, half-cleaned baby. Instead, you grab six. Shlesinger had always figured that was just how wipes worked.

“I thought, this seems really difficult, but all things are made difficult for moms, because the world hates moms,” she says. Then Pampers came to her with a campaign built on fixing that decades-long annoyance with a redesigned pack that releases one wipe at a time. The novelty of a company solving something is what stuck with her. “We live in a world where nothing gets done. And a corporation said, enough women talked to us about a problem, so we fixed it. I wish politics worked that way.”

For now she’s building the childhood she wants her kids to have, decorating for fall like there’s a neighborhood award at stake (there’s not), and processing all of it out loud for a living. Like so many of us, she still finds being a mom bewildering, but she’s doing her best nonetheless. “I’m constantly in awe of how little I know and how much I thought I knew,” she says. “Being in charge of everything, and then feeling so stupid most of the time. I think that’s peak parenting.”

#38. 250 Turkish Baby Names Inspired by Nature, Strength and Beauty

Discover the beauty, meaning, and cultural stories behind 250 captivating Turkish names.

Have you ever met someone and immediately thought, Of course that’s their name?

Maybe their name sounds soft and peaceful, and that is exactly how they carry themselves. Perhaps it feels bold and powerful, matching their confidence before they have even said a word. It can make you wonder how parents choose the perfect name for a baby they have only just met, and how they somehow know which name will grow to suit them.

Choosing a name often means imagining who that baby might become. Parents may be drawn to a particular meaning, family tradition or simply the way a name sounds, hoping it will feel right both in the first moments of life and many years later.

Names become part of how we understand people. Over time, they collect memories, personality traits, family stories and emotions. A name chosen for a newborn may begin with a meaning, a tradition or simply a beautiful sound, but it eventually becomes inseparable from the person carrying it.

Names can carry the same meaning and still sound completely different from one language to another. A name inspired by the moon may feel soft and luminous in one culture, yet bold, mysterious or quietly powerful in another.

Turkish names are especially rich in imagery. Many draw from the sky, the sea, the seasons and the natural world, turning a single word into something vivid and memorable. Aylin evokes a halo around the moon, Deniz and Derya call to mind the sea, Gunes means sun and Yildiz means star.

Others reflect qualities parents may hope their children will carry through life. Eren is associated with wisdom, Mert with bravery and honesty, and Umut with hope.

With roots in Turkic, Arabic, Persian and neighboring traditions, names used in Türkiye reflect a layered cultural history shaped by poetry, nature and generations of meaning.

Below are 100 names commonly used in Türkiye, presented in alphabetical order. The list includes feminine, masculine and gender-neutral options.

Alara – water fairy or mythic river spirit

Ebru – marbled pattern or cloudlike design

#39. Our Kids Are Growing Up Without Ever Touching Cash & It Shows

Tap, swipe, spend, repeat. Experts explain why a cashless world is making it harder to raise money-smart kids.

I’m about to reveal my age, but trust me: It’s relevant to this story. When I was growing up, my parents gave my brother and me cash. It might have been our weekly allowance or money for a Saturday afternoon at the mall, but whatever we had in our hands was our budget. There was no tapping the phone, swiping a screen, or asking Mom to Venmo us another 10 bucks.

Melissa Murphy Pavone, a certified financial planner, remembers it the same way. She recalls counting coins, organizing bills, putting money into a piggy bank, and physically handing cash to a cashier when she wanted to buy something. Her philosophy was simple: “When the money was gone, it was gone.”

But for today’s kids, that lesson is becoming increasingly harder to teach because cash is disappearing from everyday life.

Think about how different the world of money looks for Generation Z and Generation Alpha. Venmo launched in 2009, giving people a quick way to send money digitally. Apple Pay followed in 2014, allowing consumers to pay with their phones. Zelle entered the cashless arena in 2017, making it easy to transfer money directly between bank accounts. The US Mint stopped making pennies in 2025, and many companies have stopped issuing checks, replacing them with direct deposits.

With fewer people carrying cash, kids are growing up in a world where money is virtual rather than something they can hold... and moms and dads are taking notice. While some parents have tried to find humor in this growing epidemic by jumping on the "Mom Can You Send Me 4/5 Bucks" trend on TikTok, where a kid repeatedly asks their mom for varying amounts of money to a catchy jingle, others are not amused.

Jeanine Bobenmoyer, a mother of two teenagers from Indianapolis, describes the money her kids spend as invisible money. To them, she says, money doesn’t always feel real. Robbie Hyman, author of The Money Savvy Teen, agrees, saying, “There is a major difference in the way today’s teenagers experience spending money because many transactions are digital. When money is reduced to a tap, click, or swipe,” Hyman says, “children can begin to see it as more of an abstraction, and giving them access to those digital accounts can get expensive — fast.”

Bobenmoyer learned that lesson the hard way. Like many parents, she added her 15-year-old daughter to her Apple Wallet for emergencies. Instead of using it only when necessary, her daughter went on a shopping spree at Target, Sephora, Culver’s, the movies, and American Eagle. The damage? More than $1,000 in one month. Oy!

Murphy says this is a big problem. “Kids may see the purchase, but they don’t necessarily see everything behind it, such as the hours their parents worked to earn the money, the time it took to save it, or the account balance getting smaller after every purchase. Without those connections,” she says, money can feel unlimited.”

New Jersey mom Dr. Lisa Nissim has lost her patience more than once when she tried to talk to her three kids about their spending habits. The wall she’s up against is that her children have a weak understanding of money because they’ve hardly touched or managed it to pay for things, so the physical reality of what money means has diminished. Her 20-year-old son has Venmo and Zelle. Her 17-year-old daughter uses Zelle, and she describes her 13-year-old son as the Apple Pay king. Nissim says her big concern is that kids lack the knowledge that they should save money on big-ticket items, such as a car, rent, or a mortgage for a home.

Hyman puts it this way: “It’s difficult to feel ownership of something you’ve never physically experienced, and money is no exception. When a teenager’s entire experience with money is watching numbers appear and disappear on a screen, it can be much easier to spend it without thinking about what those numbers represent, and that’s not the financial habit parents want to pass down.”

Does that mean we should bring back the old mason jar method, a popular and visual way for kids to grasp budgeting, saving, and giving away money? Maybe! According to Murphy, there’s something powerful about cash. She says cash can teach children patience, limits, and trade-offs because they can physically see what they have and watch it vanish after they spend it.

The good news is it’s never too late or too early to start. Financial Coach Kristen Ricupero recommends going old school by giving children aged 3 to 10 an allowance in cash. The goal is to help them learn how to divide their money between saving, giving, and spending. For kids 10 and older, Ricupero suggests giving them cash when they go out. That way, they are forced to look at prices, make choices, and figure out what they can afford with the money in their pocket.

Murphy says parents don’t need to stop using Venmo, Apple Pay, or Zelle because technology is not the enemy. She says, “They are the tools our children will use as adults, so they need to understand how to use them responsibly. The problem,” she says, “arises when convenience replaces conversation, so start having discussions and explain how to connect the dots.”

#40. 7 Things Your Kid Wishes You Would Say More Often

The older your kids get, the harder it can be to communicate. That’s why as they grow from toddler to little kid to tween, there are some things we can remember to say to make them feel as confident as possible during those very shaky formative years. We don’t need to solve all their problems or overdirect them every single day. Some little phrases can make them (and us) slow down a little and remind our kids that nobody’s perfect, and sometimes a little kindness goes a long way.

“‘Oops’ is a very generous word. It erases blame. In a single syllable, it strengthens our relationship by affirming that we believe the other person has good intentions, even when they mess up,” says psychologist Eileen Kennedy-Moore, Ph.D. “‘Oops slows us down and reminds us not to jump to conclusions about someone’s personality when they make a mistake.” Mistakes happen, and the way we react to our children can teach them that the world isn’t perfect, and we don’t expect them to be.

As our kids get older, they need to know that we recognize they’re growing into independent beings capable of making good decisions for themselves. This may be hard for us as parents because it signifies a time when we probably need to back off a little—a time when our “babies” no longer need to be babied. “I trust you to make the decision that’s right for you” is a phrase that empowers our children to become more self-reliant.

By the time my child was three, I was already absolutely overloaded with parental advice. But one piece of wisdom that always stuck with me: the directive to avoid telling kids they’re smart.  A Stanford psychologist concluded that when children are told they are smart, they stop trying as hard. They assume intelligence and believe they don’t have to put in the work. That might be putting it too simplistically, but the intention is there; we should recognize when our kids have put in the time and reward the action. (I still tell my kids they’re smart, though, not gonna lie!)

Don’t forget to show your kid that you recognize the parts of their personality that make them a good human. When we notice things like kindness and empathy and point them out, our kids are taught that those qualities matter. And there has never been a more important time to teach our kids that those qualities matter.

When we own up to our mistakes and ask for forgiveness, we teach our kids that their mistakes will be forgiven, too. And don’t forget to own up to whatever you’re apologizing for without emphasizing your kid being too sensitive. “Apologizers are not responsible for other people’s feelings, but they are responsible for their own actions, which may have triggered those feelings. ‘I’m sorry you feel __’ implies that the other person’s feelings are the problem rather than the apologizer’s actions,” Kennedy-Moore says.

This is something adults need to hear often, too. Sometimes “finished” is more important than “perfect,” and that’s perfectly fine. Think about ways perfectionism makes your own processes more difficult; it can impose all sorts of anxiety and is the enemy of creativity. “You can help your child learn to avoid overdoing it by asking, ‘How much time is this task worth?’ Whatever your child can manage to do in that time is probably enough,” advises Kennedy-Moore. “Time is our most precious resource because we can’t get more. We don’t want to give a task more time than it deserves.”

That’s right: nothing. Sometimes what our kids need is for us to stop talking. Actively listening can be hard, but the more we attempt it, the easier it will be for our kids to trust that they can open up to us. “Active listening is a good way to improve your communication with your child,” advises the Centers for Disease Control. “It lets your child know you are interested in what she has to say.” This can be difficult for parents because we always want to “fix” everything, but sometimes the best fix is letting kids get out whatever big feelings they’re having. And they can’t do that if we don’t let them.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#44. Beautiful Eastern Orthodox Baby Names and Their Meanings

Timeless Eastern Orthodox baby names that celebrate heritage, culture, and tradition across generations

Have you ever wondered how a name can carry the weight of centuries?

When it comes to naming a baby, tradition often speaks louder than trends. For families connected to Eastern Orthodox heritage, names are more than labels. They’re echoes of centuries of culture, history, and community. These names have been passed down through generations, carrying stories of emperors, scholars, saints, and everyday people who shaped Orthodox life.

From the regal Constantine to the graceful Anastasia, this list of Eastern Orthodox baby names celebrates timeless choices that honor tradition while remaining beautiful and relevant today.

Names are more than words. They’re vessels of memory, culture, and continuity. Within Eastern Orthodox tradition, baby names reflect centuries of heritage, often inspired by Byzantine rulers, revered scholars, and beloved figures whose stories shaped communities across Greece, Russia, the Balkans, and beyond. Choosing an Orthodox baby name isn’t just about finding something elegant; it’s about honoring the past while giving your child a timeless identity that will carry meaning for generations.

From Greek Orthodox names that sparkle with classical charm to Slavic Orthodox names rooted in resilience, these choices embody tradition in its purest form. They remind us that while trends may fade, tradition endures, and a name chosen with care becomes a lasting gift.

Strong, dignified, and steeped in tradition, these boy names have been passed down through centuries of Orthodox heritage. They carry echoes of emperors, scholars, and timeless figures, making them enduring choices for families who value culture and continuity.

Aaron – Exalted, strong; St. Aaron the Priest

Abraham – Father of many; Patriarch of Israel

Achilles – Hero of the Greeks; symbol of courage

Adrian – From Hadria; St. Adrian the Martyr

Alexander – Defender of men; borne by saints and emperors

Alexios – Defender, helper; St. Alexios the Man of God

Anastasios – Resurrection; linked to Easter tradition

Anthony (Antonios) – Priceless one; St. Anthony the Great

Aristides – Best purpose; early Christian philosopher

#45. Mental health experts say you shouldn’t ban your kid from group chats. Here’s what to do instead

Group chats are often rife with bullying, exclusion and inappropriate content. Here's how to teach kids to use them wisely.

By Lauren Ramakrishna Updated Oct. 12, 2026

I’ll never forget the day my seventh grader got off the school bus with his head hung, walking at a snail’s pace up to the house. “What’s wrong, bud?” I asked. “Mom, I don’t want to wear my new shoes to school anymore.”

We bought those shoes the night before and he was ecstatic about them. They were flashy for sure—bright neon yellow covering every inch—but he absolutely loved them.

“What happened?” I asked. “The kids on the bus were making fun of them,” he replied. “And then one of the kids in my grade showed me that people were talking about them in the group chat.”

The group chat. I’d heard about it before. It started around fifth grade and had only grown as more and more kids got cell phones. My smartwatch-wearing son wasn’t in it, but that didn’t save him from falling victim to group chat bullying.

His experience follows a trend that pediatric mental health experts know all too well. “I commonly see increased anxiety, fear of missing out, disrupted sleep, social comparison, and increased peer conflict connected to group-chat activity,” says Cara Toretta, MD, an adolescent psychiatrist and Director of Silver Hill Hospital’s adolescent residential program in New Canaan, Connecticut.

Yet Dr. Toretta and other experts acknowledge that group chats aren’t all bad. “The benefit is that group chats can support friendships, social connection and coordination around school and activities,” Dr. Toretta says.

So, what’s a parent to do? Your instinct may be to forbid group chats outright, but experts agree that’s not the way to go. “Banning your kids from group chats could make them feel isolated and resentful toward you,” advises Vinay Saranga, MD, a child and adolescent psychiatrist and founder of Saranga Comprehensive Psychiatry in Apex, North Carolina.

“From a mental health perspective, a gradual approach with supervision, clear expectations and boundaries, and ongoing conversations is often more effective than unrestricted access or an outright ban,” Dr. Toretta adds.

Think of the group chat as another space for social learning. “Group chats give children a real-life window into group dynamics, peer pressure, and what we call the groupthink mentality—that feeling that you need to go along with the group in order to belong,” says Liz Nissim, Ph.D., a psychologist at Psychological and Educational Consulting in Livingston, New Jersey.

If you approach group chats with care, they can become a space where kids can practice relationship-building skills, boundary setting, how to navigate peer pressure, and build their own identities, Dr. Nissim says.

That’s clearly a necessary skill, sadly illustrated by the devastating events at Cornell University. Members of the Chi Phi fraternity posted pictures and derogatory language in a group chat, announcing that an intoxicated female student was sexually available. Not a single member of the group chat was brave enough to intervene, notify the authorities or even express disapproval. Now the student, known as Jane Doe, is suing Cornell University, the Chi Phi fraternity chapter at Cornell, and seven student members of the fraternity who she alleges participated in her gang rape.

“This story definitely reinforces that we need to teach these skills before kids are in the middle of a difficult group chat situation. They need to know what is clearly inappropriate and be ready to make smart choices when these situations arise,” Dr. Saranga says.

Learning how to handle difficult group chat situations develops skills that transfer beyond their digital life. “Teaching children how to pause before responding, consider how their words might affect someone else, recognize when a conversation has crossed a line, and have the confidence to step away are skills that will serve them far beyond the group chat,” Dr. Nissim says.

Assess your child’s responses to social situations that happen offline. Are they able to handle disagreement, stand up for themselves, and pull away from group activities when they start to head in a bad direction? These skills are necessary to make the jump to online discourse.

Dr. Toretta says other signs of readiness include the ability to follow family technology rules and seek help when something uncomfortable happens. “A child or teen who can tolerate feeling left out without becoming consumed by it and who shows kindness and good judgment is often better prepared for the challenges of group-chat participation,” she adds.

“Before giving a child that access, parents should have conversations about digital citizenship, privacy, kindness, peer pressure, and what to do when a conversation crosses a line,” Dr. Nissim advises.

Saranga says it’s wise to come up with potential scenarios your kids might encounter in group chats—gossip, bullying, inappropriate content, conflict—and discuss how they should handle them.

Begin with a smaller group chat with your child’s closest friends so they can dip a toe in the shallow end before trying to wade in the deep end.

“I think it’s a smart idea to start slow,” Dr. Saranga shares. “Before you allow your kids to chat with friends on all different platforms whenever they want, start with one platform and set a time limit of maybe 20 or 30 minutes per day so they have to prove they can handle it. Then you can slowly raise the limits.”

Don’t monitor every message going in and out. Instead you should check in with your child about what’s happening in the chat, the topics of discussion, how people are responding, and how your child feels about the chat, Dr. Nissim says. “The goal is to help children develop the judgment to manage these conversations independently, not to make them feel that an adult has to monitor every interaction forever,” she explains.

As you have these conversations, take advantage of opportunities to react to teachable moments. “We want children to learn that they don’t have to participate in every conversation, they don’t have to agree with the group, and they don’t have to stay in a space that makes them uncomfortable,” Dr. Nissim says.

Group chats can also help kids understand the nuances of digital communications, which lack the body language and other context clues of real-world interactions. Leadership expert Tara Furiani recalls a time when her daughters and their friends were playing a pretend game involving a “hostage.” “One of my daughters went to the group chat and said, ‘I know where you live.’ In the context of their game, it was pretend. Another mom understandably read it very differently when going through her daughter’s phone later,” Furiani says. While she was able to clear up the confusion with the other parent quickly, she used the incident as a teachable moment with her kids, ages 15, 13, 12, 9 and 9.

“I don’t expect a child to instinctively understand how something that made sense in a game could sound threatening on a screen. That’s something we have to teach,” she says.

If grades are falling, your child’s behavior changes, or they seem disconnected or depressed, something happening in the group chat could be to blame. “These are all signs that parents need to intervene,” Dr. Saranga says.

If your child comes to you to talk about hurtful interactions they had in the chat (or even just heard about, like my son), respond with interest and care. “Be curious with your child about what happened, help them put the experience in perspective, reinforce healthy friendships, and intervene with the school when the behavior crosses into bullying or significantly impacts their emotional well-being,” Dr. Toretta says.

Just because you make a decision to allow group chats doesn’t mean you can’t take it back. If you notice that participating in the chat negatively impacts your child’s happiness or discover they aren’t following your family’s expectations while chatting, it’s okay to put a pause on group chats.

Sometimes technology can be your friend. Parental apps like Bark and Quistodio use AI to scan your kids’ messages, flag potential risks and send you alerts when something concerning happens.

Or there’s Moxies, a research-backed social platform for girls ages 8–12, designed to help them learn how to be good digital citizens and practice digital communication with real-life friends through small, private, parent-approved groups. It was founded by Juliette Blake, a mom of three, who spent more than 20 years working the youth digital media landscape.

It’s important to remember that you should use these tools to flag particularly egregious or dangerous behavior while your child develops the skills to become their own group chat supervisor. It’s OK, and even advisable, to back away as your child proves they can handle group chat access without constant parental oversight.

My own experience with my son’s group chat struggle led to a valuable conversation about groupthink bullying, peer pressure, individual expression, and determining who is a real friend. I gave my son the space to express his disappointment and hurt, and a really hard moment brought us even closer. Plus, he knows he can come to me with hard conversations about group chats and I won’t fly off the handle.

He took a day off from his new shoes. But by day two post drama, they were back on his feet.
