#46. 23 Cheap Recipes To Feed A Crowd, Since It's Gathering Season

Use when the whole gang’s in town and they’ll be here at 6 o’clock.

Your family is in town. Your group of girlfriends is coming over for book club. Your neighbors are en route to watch the big game. Your teen’s four besties from school are coming over to work on a project. Whatever the case may be, you need some cheap recipes to feed a crowd that won’t break the bank or take forever to get on the table. When I think about some potentially easy meals for large family gatherings, I lean toward things that yield a lot of food (obviously), and that do it with a relatively short ingredient list so I’m not blowing my grocery budget on one dinner. And ideally, they’d be things that tend to be crowd-pleasers, or something (like the burger bowls below) where I can set out all the toppings and let each person customize their meal. These recipes do all of that for the least amount of moola possible.

Let’s say it’s a couple days after Thanksgiving and you’re still swimming in leftover turkey and houseguests. Princess Pinky Girl’s turkey biscuit stew is an easy and affordable way to reuse your cooked turkey but make it into a simple pot pie style that tastes new.

I love a good chicken thigh recipe, especially because they’re on sale so often at the grocery stores where I live. These red curry chicken thighs from All The Healthy Things only require a few seasonings to dress them up, and she serves them with a simple garlic rice and spicy cucumber salad.

If you need a vat of pulled chicken for tacos, enchiladas, or rice bowls, Princess Pinky Girl’s recipe will get the job done for you. All you need is a slow cooker, two pounds of chicken breasts or tenders, taco seasoning, two cups of salsa, and the juice of one lime (but even that is kind of optional).

Tilapia is the most affordable fish, especially if you buy the frozen filets (I lived on them when I was single). Damn Delicious’ sheet pan recipe calls for simple roast veggie sides to pair with them, so all in all this meal feels a lil’ fancy but is budget-friendly.

Ground beef is one of those things most families keep in the fridge, which means spaghetti, tacos, or burgers are evergreen options. If you want to change it up just a little, you could make All The Healthy Things’ burger bowls, which give you the same classic flavor combos of a burger but over greens instead of on a bun.

Damn Delicious’ spaghetti aglio e olio is cheap cheap — a super-affordable 30-minute meal of pasta topped with breadcrumbs, garlic, Parmesan, olive oil, salt, pepper, and red pepper flakes. Serve it with a salad and you’re golden, I say.

Family Fresh Meals’ Chicago Italian beef sandwiches basically cook themselves, and you get a bunch of food for the minimal effort this recipe requires. Serve this on toasted hoagies with provolone and a side of chips and call it good.

The heartier version of spaghetti looks like this: Tessie’s Table’s baked spaghetti, which yields a baking dish full of cheesy, meat-saucy pasta that will satisfy many a hungry house guest. The ingredients are all affordable and there aren’t many of them, but the meal you get out of them is so good.

Listen, most food websites will tell you the only salads worth serving guests have like 18 ingredients, and most of them are exotic stone fruits you can’t find at a Walmart. But let’s be real — there’s a reason people love the simplicity of, say, Olive Garden’s endless salad. Princess Pinky Girl’s lemon parm salad kind of recreates that magic. You need precious few ingredients, and it will go with quite literally anything you choose to serve alongside it.

Who doesn’t love a low country boil with Old Bay-seasoned shrimp, corn, and potatoes? (Personally, I love when you can fish a whole head of garlic out and spread the cloves on the potatoes.) Budget Bytes’ recipe breaks down how to make one if it’s your first time. This recipe feeds six and clocks in at $2.76 per serving.

Think a Hamburger Helper-like meal, but with a tortilla chip crunch — that’s Damn Delicious’ one-pot nacho beef skillet for you. The ingredient list looks a little long but it’s mostly seasonings you likely have anyway, and you could definitely buy just one type of cheese instead of two.

Boneless skinless chicken tenders, Hawaiian rolls, a jar of marinara — the ingredients list in Fresh Apron’s recipe is short and all on the affordable side. But what you get is an entire slab of little mini chicken parm sandwiches with all the saucy, cheesy goodness you expect.

Averie Cooks’ barbecue chicken skillet is so incredibly simple, it only takes 15 minutes to turn a handful of ingredients into a proper meal. Serve this over mac and cheese, alongside some roasted potatoes and green beans, or in a wrap.

This one-skillet recipe from Averie Cooks has a very short ingredient list and only takes 20 minutes to make. This recipe yields four servings, so you may want to double it up for your crowd — they’ll definitely want seconds of this spicy, sweet combo.

There’s arguably no better affordable dish than beans and rice. It’s got protein, fiber, carbs — it’s a complete meal, nutritionally speaking. It’s great if you need a base for chicken or beef, a side for a crowd, or all on its own, and this recipe from Tessie’s Table will help you make it flavorful and fork-tender.

Ground turkey is usually a lot cheaper than ground beef, probably because it tends to dry out easily while cooking. But when you put it in a dish like chili, well, that takes care of that problem. Fresh Apron’s turkey and bean chili is a cheap crowd-pleaser, and people love filing down the counter in a line choosing their toppings.

Six servings for 90 cents a piece? You can’t beat Budget Bytes’ potato soup recipe for budget-friendliness. This recipe is easy to scale up to feed more guests, and everyone loves potato soup, so it’s a solid crowd-pleasing pick.

Everyone likes baked potatoes, and they are blessedly cheap. Make everyone their own potato and lay out the butter, cheese, bacon bits, and whatever other toppings you like so everyone can DIY their dinner. Princess Pinky Girl’s recipe explains how to do it in the air fryer.

Sheet pan nachos, like these from My Casual Pantry, are so fun to serve and just let everyone dig in. If you want to use up leftover chicken, you can shred it and toss it on, or use any cut of chicken you can find on sale really. How fancy or elaborate you get with the toppings is entirely up to you and your budget.

If everyone’s coming over for breakfast, a casserole like this one from Budget Bytes is definitely the move. It’s described as cheesy, flavorful, and filling (sign me up), and looks like it would have the most satisfying crunch thanks to the tortilla chip topping.

Potatoes, onions, and eggs — that’s the base of this crispy potato kugel from A Sweet Thyme that makes 12 servings to dish out. It’s onion-y, garlic-y, and so delicious. Serve it with literally anything; you will hear zero complaints.

Bucket List Tummy’s sheet pan kielbasa and veggies are ready in 50 minutes start to finish, and 40 minutes of that time is spent in the oven. That means you can make a whole bunch of food for a little bit of money, and still spend your time actually enjoying your house guests rather than cooking the time away.

Budget Bytes’ cheese enchilada recipe serves four people if each guest eats three enchiladas. But her recipe has a helpful feature where you can edit the number of servings you want to make, and it will adjust your shopping list accordingly (hallelujah, you don’t have to do fractions in your head).

Whatever you serve your guests, they’re sure to taste the love in every bite.

This article was originally published on November 18, 2025

#50. Get Into a Back-to-School Mindset With Advice From 12 Youth Soccer Coaches

Start the school year off on the right foot with insights from coaches who understand how the game translates to life off the field.

Late summer is always the hardest on parents. The pool days are numbered. The long evenings are shortening. The school year is coming, and it doesn’t care how ready you are.

The back-to-school transition is never the clean handoff the calendar makes it look like. Every August, we tell ourselves this year will be different. You’ll get ahead of it. Lunch prep sorted by Sunday. Bedtime routine locked in a week early. Screen-time rules clearly communicated and actually enforced. You’ll draw up this plan with the kind of granular, paranoid attention to detail that Guardiola brings to a cup final. But then, it’s all a disaster by Tuesday.

If you’re looking for an actual strategy that holds up, go to the park on a Saturday morning, find the sideline, and start listening to whoever is coaching.

These are people managing every extreme of human emotion — low blood sugar, wounded pride, full-on existential crises — all while trying to stop a five-way argument over who gets the neon green goalie pinnies. If they don’t know something useful, nobody does. So we hit up a dozen youth soccer coaches for their best back-to-school advice.

I tell my girls this on the first day of every season, and I mean it every time. Some days we’re doing your favorite thing. Some days we’re doing the thing you hate. The thing you hate is usually the thing that needs work. That’s not a coincidence. I don’t let them skip the hard drills because they don’t feel like it. I don’t let them drift to the stuff they’re already good at and call it practice. That’s not practice. That’s just playing around.

The subject your kid is dreading going back to — that’s the one. That’s the drill they need to run. Don’t negotiate them out of it. Make the deal: Do the work first, then we talk. It’s the same conversation I have at practice every Tuesday and Thursday, and it works there, too.

I don’t do big speeches. I never have. I’ve seen coaches do the whole thing — the whiteboard, the clipboard, the fire-and-brimstone season opener — and the kids are bored by the second sentence. So I just ask one question: What kind of teammate do you want? And they tell me. Funny. Helpful. Somebody who doesn’t make you feel bad when you mess up. Somebody who actually passes the ball. I write it all down. Then I say, good — now be all of that.

It’s not complicated. It’s just that nobody asks them the question directly and then holds them to the answer. Try it before school starts. Ask your kid what kind of friend they want to have this year. Then have the second half of that conversation.

I’ve been doing this since before most of these parents were driving their kids to practice, and the one thing that has never changed is this: Effort is the one thing every single kid controls completely. Talent, you’re born with, or you’re not. Height, same thing. But running back on defense when you’re tired? Picking yourself up after a bad touch and going again? That’s a choice. I’ve had kids with every physical tool in the world coast through and wonder why they weren’t improving. I’ve had kids who couldn’t trap a ball if their life depended on it go on to be captains because they simply refused to stop working.

Teachers see it the same way I do. The kid who stays after, asks questions, turns things in on time — that kid builds a reputation. And that reputation opens doors that talent alone doesn’t.

Every season, I get at least one kid who shows up on day one with opinions. Wants to play a different position, run a different shape, do things the way her last team did it. And look — I love that. I want players who think about the game. But there’s an order of operations. You don’t get to redesign a system you don’t understand yet. So the rule is: First month, you learn why we do what we do. Why we press from the front. Why we switch the point of attack the way we do.

Once you understand the why, then you’ve earned the right to push back.

A new school year means new teachers with their own ways of doing things. The kid who spends the first few weeks actually paying attention — figuring out how this classroom works before deciding what they think of it — that kid is so far ahead of the one who comes in with their arms already crossed.

I have a rule on this team, and it has been the same rule since my first season: You get three seconds after a mistake. Three seconds to be upset, to be frustrated, to feel whatever you feel. Then your head comes back up, and you get back in position. Because here’s the thing: The play is still happening. The game didn’t stop because you had a bad touch. And if you’re standing there feeling sorry for yourself, you’re now two mistakes deep instead of one.

I tell parents this, too, because it applies to everything. Your kid is going to fail a test this year. They’re going to say something wrong in class and feel embarrassed about it. They’re going to have a bad day. In life situations off the field, you get more than three seconds, but the same lesson applies. Acknowledge the mistake and then head up, back in position. The recovery is the name of the game.

I am obsessive about communication on the field. Obsessive. Not yelling, not blaming — information. Constant, useful, real-time information between players. Where you are, what you see, what they should do next. Most kids go completely silent under pressure, and that is exactly backwards from what you need. When it’s hardest to talk is when talking matters most.

I tell my players: A quiet team is a confused team. And a confused team gives the ball away. It’s the same thing off the field. The kid who speaks up in class, who says hi to the kid sitting alone at lunch, who tells a friend when something’s wrong — that kid ends up in the middle of things. The good things. Make some noise this year. Say something.

I played college soccer, and I will tell you that the thing nobody taught me until it was almost too late was how to rest. We were all conditioned to think that more was always better — more sprints, more film, more time in the gym. And there’s a point where more just breaks you. The best thing I ever did for my game was learn to take recovery seriously. Sleep. Real sleep. Not optional, not a treat — part of the program.

I build rest into my players’ weeks now, and I don’t let them feel guilty about it. The brain works the same way the body does. It consolidates everything it learned while you sleep. So if your kid is heading back to school and you’re letting them stay up until midnight on their phone — that’s not a small thing. That’s undermining everything they did that day. Rest is not laziness. I promise you it’s not.

I’ve been watching kids show up to this field for a long time, and I can tell you — the ones who get there early are different. Not because they’re more talented. Because they’ve had time to settle in. They’ve already touched a ball, already talked to a teammate, already figured out where they are and what they’re doing before anything’s officially started. They’re comfortable. The ones sprinting in right at the whistle are always the ones who take the whole first half to find their rhythm.

So on the first day of school, get there early. Your kid will have the chance to find the right classroom, ask any questions, and breathe a little bit. It’s a small thing that changes the whole morning.

I coach little kids. Eight-year-olds. So I see a lot of feelings on this field, and I’ve been real clear about my policy since day one: All the feelings are allowed. You can cry. You can tell me you need a minute. You can be upset. None of that is a problem. What you cannot do is walk off this field and decide you’re done. That’s the one thing I won’t accept. And I don’t say it mean — I just say it clearly, and I say it early, so it’s already been said when the moment comes.

Back to school is hard for a lot of kids, and I think parents sometimes feel like they’re supposed to pretend it isn’t. The anxiety is real. The overwhelm is real. Your kid can feel all of it and still go. That’s actually the lesson — that you’re allowed to struggle and still show up. Those two things can both be true at the same time.

I think about the game the way I think about conversation. There are moments when you have to speak — when you see the opening, and you have to take it, because if you wait, it’ll be gone. And there are moments when the best thing you can do is find the person in a better position and give it to them. The hardest thing to coach is the judgment between those two moments. A player who always shoots is a ball hog. A player who always passes is invisible. The great ones — the really great ones — know the difference in real time.

That’s an ego conversation as much as it’s a soccer conversation. Knowing when to speak up in class and when to let someone else take the floor. When to lead a group project and when to step back and support. It’s one of the harder things to teach, and one of the more important ones. Start having that conversation now, before the year starts.

I want my players to come to me. That’s the whole thing. I make myself as available as I possibly can because I know from experience that the kids who ask questions are the ones who get better. Not always the most talented kids — just the ones who seek feedback and then actually do something with it. Every season, the gap I notice most isn’t about skill. It’s about which kids advocate for themselves and which ones wait to be noticed.

Teachers work the same way I do. They want to help — they really do — but they’re managing a roomful of kids, and they can’t chase all of them down. The ones who stay after, send the email, ask what they missed and what they can do better — those are the ones who get more of the good stuff. It’s not about being the favorite. It’s about knowing how to ask for help. That skill will serve your kid for the rest of their life.

I coach at the level where it starts to get serious. Parents are thinking about high school rosters, kids are thinking about highlight reels, everybody’s tracking individual stats. And I am here to tell you — from where I stand on this sideline — that the players who make the biggest difference are almost never the ones you’d expect.

I’ve had physically gifted kids who played every game like it was an audition and made everyone around them worse for it. And I’ve had kids who, by every measurable standard, were average, who won us games because they made their teammates better. They covered for people, they communicated, and they did the stuff that doesn’t show up in the box score.

We spend so much time on our kids as individuals — their grades, their performance, their future — that we sometimes forget to teach them how to be good at being part of something. That’s a skill too. Maybe the most important one. The school year is long and almost entirely a team sport. Remind them.

#52. 43 Horse Girl Names For The Kid You’re Already Signing Up For Riding Lessons

Growing up, every grade school class had at least one: a horse girl. You know the type. Her pride and joy was her full Breyer collection, and she was rarely spotted without a dog-eared copy of Misty of Chincoteague in her bag. Maybe that girl was you. Maybe it still is! And, truly, there’s no shame in that. While “horse girl” used to be a playground insult, the equestrian aesthetic is full-on mainstream now.

So, if you’ve got a horse girl’s heart and a baby on the way, why not lean all the way in? Can’t you just picture your tiny equestrian now, bundled up in a barn jacket? These baby names pull from horse etymology, legendary steeds, breeds, barn life, and, of course, iconic horse girls (real and fictional).

I mean, it’s Greek for “lover of horses,” which pretty much makes this the OG horse girl name. It’s polished and a little regal, with the bonus of having Pippa right there as a nickname.

I’ve always loved how romantic and Shakespearean this name is! But it’s also secretly equestrian, as it comes from Germanic roots meaning “horse” and “tender.”

Not up on your Welsh mythology? Don’t worry; I’ve got you: Rhiannon was a queen who rode a white horse no one could catch. Not surprisingly, this name means “divine queen.”

Epona, the Celtic goddess of horses, was so beloved that Roman cavalry soldiers adopted her as their own. In ancient Gaulish, the name means “great mare.”

This wholesome name means “grace,” but real horse girls know it’s a nod to Wild West sharpshooter and icon Annie Oakley.

If you gravitate toward gender-neutral options, consider Ryder! It means “mounted warrior” or “horseman” and has a cool rodeo energy.

The Morgan is one of America’s oldest horse breeds, and it all started with a single stallion named Figure. Another gender-neutral option, this Welsh name means “born of the sea.”

Percy is short for Percheron, a powerful, elegant French draft horse breed. It means “one who pierces the valley” and is just preppy enough to have built-in book-nerd cred.

Obviously, right?! This name, which means “filled with a light haze,” is for anyone who wore out their copy of Marguerite Henry’s 1947 classic about a Chincoteague pony. Just pure nostalgia in name form.

If you love lore, this name’s for you: Zenyatta is the legendary mare who won 19 races in a row and became the first female horse to win the Breeders’ Cup Classic. Nickname options are plentiful, but I’m partial to Zenny.

This name may be Spanish for “dove,” but it sounds an awful lot like palomino: the golden-coated horse with a flaxen mane. It’s so pretty and makes for a great subtle horse girl nod.

Calling all lovers of one-syllable names! Let’s file this one under coastal equestrian chic because, well, a bay conjures up images of a quaint coastal town… but also a bay horse has a reddish-brown coat with black points.

While we’re talking horse-hair colors, add Roan to your shortlist. A roan-coated horse has white hairs mixed in with the base color, so it looks almost frosted. I love how earthy and unexpected and Irish this name feels.

Like rein, but make it a name. See what we did there? This name of French origin primarily means “queen” and would also make a great middle moniker.

If you want something super unique, look to this derivative of Xanthos: Achilles’ immortal horse in the Iliad, who could actually speak. Of Greek origin, the name means “golden” or “fair-haired.”

Any horse girl who read the Thoroughbred series knows that Ashleigh Griffen was practically the patron saint of horse girls. Meaning “dweller near the ash tree forest,” this name feels feminine and classic.

Stevie Lake was the loud, funny member of The Saddle Club, so if you were a horse girl in the ‘90s, you know exactly why this name made the list.

Zara Tindall is a horse girl like her mom, Princess Anne! The latter competed in eventing at the 1976 Montreal Olympics, while her daughter won Olympic silver in eventing at the 2012 London Olympics. Plus, how pretty is it that this name means “blooming flower” in Arabic?

Ugh, I’m obsessed with names that sound like nicknames you’d give to that one friend everyone loves, and Beezie definitely qualifies. This name is, of course, a nod to show-jumping legend Beezie Madden.

If you’re a real glutton for punishment, you could borrow this name from Atreyu’s horse in The NeverEnding Story. Too soon? Never.

#53. The Yoto Player 4th Gen just dropped. Here’s what’s different

The Yoto Player 4th Gen comes with the biggest hardware upgrade in the company's history, three years in the making.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 09, 2026

While there are other storytelling players on the market, Yoto has long been a top pick with parents. It’s durable, multi-functional and — if judged by dollars-to-minutes spent — worth its weight in gold.

For the uninitiated, the design is simple. Kids insert their own content cards to listen to a huge and ever-growing library of bestselling audiobooks, music and singalongs, educational activities and podcasts. The library runs from little-kid faves like Peppa Pig, Mo Willems and The Wiggles to classics that keep older kids equally engaged like Harry Potter and A Series of Unfortunate Events. The cards take up minimal space, and because the content is also available on the parent app, losing a card never means losing the story. It also functions as a night light, room thermometer, white noise machine, clock and sleep trainer, and it comes with a record-your-own card for the books they request on loop.

My own now-teenager had the original model for years before passing it down to a younger cousin, with a sweet message recorded onto one of those make-your-own cards. Honestly, any toy that outlasts a single childhood — especially a tech-based one — is so refreshing.

Now there’s a new Yoto in town. The Yoto Player 4th Gen arrives in October, and it comes with the biggest hardware upgrade in the company’s history, three years in the making. It’s available to pre-order now at $149.99, with shipping expected to start October 15.

The most obvious update is a new Green Button. Parents can load up to 20 favorite stories, songs, podcasts or soundscapes into the Yoto app ahead of time, and kids twist and press to play them instantly, no card required. For independent players who want to start their own listening without hunting down a card first, it’s a great upgrade. (And let’s be real. It absolves you of panic-hunting for their favorite story card 15 minutes past bedtime.)

Then there’s the changes you can’t see. They’ve doubled the storage to 64GB, which, according to Yoto, holds more than 1,000 hours of audio. A new processer means stories and music now download about ten times faster than on the old model. As far as sound, audiophile parents will appreciate the upgraded acoustically engineered stereo speaker. Even the night light got a glow up. (Sorry, we had to.) The display is now a full panel with seven colors, adjustable brightness, and day-and-night modes that shift the light, clock cues and OK-to-Wake signal as the day moves from morning podcast to bedtime wind-down. Like previous generations, it charges via USB-C or wireless, running up to 16 hours on one charge.

Almost all of your existing cards will play on the 4th Gen, so your collection carries over. However, Yoto has said the functionality on Interactive Yoto cards isn’t live yet on the new platform, since the 4th Gen runs on entirely new technology. They’re currently working on rebuilding existing features so hopefully it’s just a temporary inconvenience. For most families with a stack of stories and music cards, nothing changes. (Find out more about which interactive cards are affected here.)

This is where Yoto crushes the game. The design is age-universal in a way very few kids’ products manage to pull off. It’s as at home with a 3-year-old sounding out their first audiobook as it is with a 12-year-old working through a chapter series at bedtime. (Or sulking in their room and listening to music, if we’re being realistic.)

Choosing a winner is a bit like comparing a regular pizza to a personal pan pizza. A matter or preference and use case, if you will. The full-size Yoto Player 4th Gen ($149.99) is the home base, with the night light, clock and bigger sound for the nightstand. The Yoto Mini 4th Gen ($109.99) is the smaller, more rugged travel version, now rated for splashes and dust and built to live in a backpack. Plenty of families own both.

If you’re new to Yoto, the 4th Gen is the best version of a product parents universally love. If you’re a current owner, upgrading isn’t a must. Yes, the updates are impressive, but knowing what we know about Yoto, your older version is likely still in perfect working order. Of course if there’s an adorable cousin to hand it down to, giving your household a good excuse to upgrade, go forth. Just be sure to record something special on a record-your-own card before you pass it on.

#56. 10 Great Sports Docs & True-Life Stories To Stream With Your Kids Right Now

From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.

Finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough. But if you’ve got a sporty kid, screen time is a great opportunity. Sure, there’s old-school sports movie like The Sandlot or A League of Their Own — complete with inspirational messages and strong moral codes. But why go for fictional sports stories when you can get the real thing?

Sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes. They tell inspirational tales and maybe even give them a real-life role model in the meantime. From a variety of different sports to a selection of different formats, we’ve thought about the watchability and the relevance of each of these selections. There should be something for everyone in this list. And, at the very least, with each, you and your kid will learn something.

This documentary film focuses on several different Paralympic athletes, all of whom have truly amazing stories. Warning for parents: This documentary is not for the faint of heart, as some of the physical challenges are truly harrowing. For example, Bebe Vio — who inspired the name of the documentary — lost all of her limbs to meningitis at the age of 11. She nonetheless went on to become a wheelchair fencer. Deeply inspiring, this doc is great for teens interested in sports and perhaps great for all of us to have a little perspective on the amazing nature of the human spirit.

The 2004 story of the Boston Red Sox is a great one in terms of an underdog story. Even if you’re not a Red Sox fan, this story represents a very specific time in baseball and tells the story of how this iconic team broke a curse that had existed since 1918. If your kid is just starting to get into baseball, this documentary series might seem like ancient history; after all, 2004 was more than 20 years ago. And yet, this particular season for many of us feels very recent and still relevant.

Who doesn’t love trick shots? This 30 for 30 ESPN doc is all about a group of five guys who were former college roommates who created a sports comedy entertainment phenomenon. Focused on trick shots and betting, this doc is 100% for older kids. But if you’ve got a teen who is into sports and loves to joke around, this is a great, quirky documentary focused on male friendship, humor, and creating something nobody has ever done before.

Everybody is obsessed with Travis Kelce, but his brother Jason Kelce might be the more interesting of the siblings, at least as an athlete. The 2023 documentary film chronicles the 2022 Philadelphia Eagles season, with a specific focus on Kelce. The main tension here is whether or not Kelce will retire from the NFL. Weird topic for kids? Well, for tweens and teens interested in unpacking the real-deal toll of being in the NFL, there’s something smartly educational about this. You may be young and obsessed with football now, but life is long.

Not technically a documentary, this is a docudrama based on the true story of Ray McElrathbey, who deals with a ton of family adversity and racism. Set in the early 2000s, McElrathbey’s story is inspiring and very family-oriented. Again, this one might be for older kids, but the script is from Nick Santora of Reacher and Sopranos fame, so there’s a breezy and very focused feeling to this movie.

Here’s another docudrama that is based on a real-life movement in India, centered on teenagers and skateboarding culture. In the film, a young girl named Prerna (Rachel Sanchita Gupta) finds purpose and belonging through skateboarding. The film is a heartwarming coming-of-age movie, but watching it with your kid means you’re also giving them a dose of contemporary history. The production for the film also worked very closely with rural villages in India to make sure it accurately portrayed the culture and struggles of teenagers.

A great one to watch with your aspiring skateboarding kid, or maybe a kid who isn’t sure what their athletic interest might be.

One of the greatest athletes of our time is also the subject of a one-of-a-kind docuseries. Released in 2024, Simone Biles Rising is all about the gymnast’s comeback. The fact that Biles has been so transparent about her mental health has been a groundbreaking part of the conversations about young athletes. As both a role model and someone who is part of living history, Biles is a figure that should inspire conversation with your curious athlete.

This 10-part documentary changed everything back in 2020. However, at this point, The Last Dance — which tells the story of one of the greatest periods of the Chicago Bulls — almost feels vintage. Chances are, for certain parents, you didn’t have a kid old enough to watch this documentary nearly seven years ago. And, if you’re of the generation that lived through the Bulls’ 1990s dynasty, then you owe it to share that history with your kid.

Not everything about Michael Jordan and his teammates is admirable, to be clear. But the thing about some great sports history is that it can be messy.

Focused on the 2024 X Games, The Rise: Gold Medal Girls of the X Games focuses on four teen athletes, Arisa Trew, Shiloh Catori, Reese Nelson, and Jada Ward. Those are all skateboarders, and that’s just the most recent season. More broadly, The Rise covers all sorts of women’s sports, from skating to the WNBA. If you have a young woman looking for some new role models, you can’t miss with the various seasons of The Rise.

You can really start anywhere with this excellent docuseries. But the most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained is focused on the 2024 Tour de France. Obviously, the famous bicycle race has existed since 1903, but it’s really only recently that we could actually document this incredible event. Even the least sporty kid in the world can get excited about people using their bodies to propel a bicycle forward. And the most sporty kids will have trouble wrapping their mind around the sheer effort it takes to traverse 2,200 miles over 24 days over some of the hilliest terrain on Earth.

The most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained, released in 2025, is now the last season of this docuseries. The real Tour de France hasn’t gone anywhere, of course. In fact, it’s happening right now. Meaning if you get your kid excited enough, you can watch the 2026 Tour de France as it’s happening. Or watch a little contemporary Tour de France, then go back and watch Unchained on Netflix.

#59. The Baby Rash Nobody Warns You About

Somewhere around month three, your baby turns into a tiny, adorable faucet. Bibs get soaked, shirts get soaked, you get soaked. And one morning you notice a patch of red, bumpy skin around their mouth and chin that wasn’t there yesterday. Meet drool rash: common, not contagious, and very fixable. Here’s how to spot it, soothe it, and keep it from coming back.

Drool rash shows up as flat or slightly raised red patches, sometimes with small bumps, sometimes looking dry and chapped. It usually lands wherever saliva sits: around the mouth, on the chin and cheeks, and in the folds of the neck. If your baby soaks through their clothes, it can show up on the chest too.

It can look alarming, but it isn’t contagious and isn’t a sign of a serious health problem. It can make your baby uncomfortable, though, so it’s worth treating.

The cause is simple: skin that stays wet with saliva for long stretches gets irritated. A few things make that more likely:

Most drool rash clears up with care at home. The goal is clean, dry, and protected skin.

You can’t stop the drool (and you shouldn’t: saliva helps babies swallow, softens first foods, and protects new teeth). But you can keep it from sitting on the skin.

Your pediatrician may suggest an over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream or prescribe one. Don’t start a steroid cream on your baby’s face without their OK.

See a doctor sooner if the rash comes with a fever, unusual tiredness, or trouble breathing or swallowing.

It’s also worth a check-in if you’re not sure it’s drool rash at all. A rash that won’t budge can sometimes be a skin infection or eczema, which look similar but need different treatment, and there’s also the chance of hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). Your doctor can tell them apart.

The drool era feels endless when you’re on your fourth bib by lunch. But like so many baby phases, it’s gone before you know it. As teething winds down and the drooling slows, the rash usually fades with it. One day the bibs are back in the drawer, and their chin is finally dry.

So while you’re dabbing that chin, grab a photo of their gummy, glistening grin too. In a year, you’ll be glad you saved it.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#60. Parenting A Neurodivergent Kid Has Never Been This Loud. Here's How To Cut Through The Noise

Stay away from the misinformation and get expert-reviewed info at Understood.org.

Whether it’s coming from loud posts in your social feed, wild headlines in your inbox, or your neighbor who pays too much attention to both, commentary on neurodivergence is everywhere.

For those of us trying to raise a kid who learns or thinks differently, reliable, practical, non-scary information and advice can be hard to find. In fact, 52% of videos about ADHD and 41% of videos about autism on TikTok are inaccurate or misleading, according to a recent analysis. And that misleading intel can add to confusion: A survey of caregivers conducted by an Ohio Children’s hospital found that one in four regretted a health decision they made for their child based on conflicting information.

It’s tough out here. But maybe you’ve heard of Understood.org, the non-profit organization created to support the neurodivergent community, including parents of neurodivergent kiddos (who might be neurodivergent themselves). Their content covers conditions like ADHD, dyslexia, and other language and processing disorders. Understood has no pharmaceutical backing, and they’re not selling anything. Everything they provide is free and expert-reviewed at a time when truth is in short supply.What’s more, all of their advice, articles, podcasts, and products are based on quality research and vetted by actual experts in education, healthcare, and research. That means you won’t lose hours falling into a fact-checking rabbit hole, or wind up second-guessing a decision you made based on misinformation. Despite all the noise, no one is ultimately accountable for the outcome of our choices except us — and that makes trustworthy information all the more valuable.

If you’ve been feeling overwhelmed, you’re not alone. Here are some key ways to get reliable information you can trust and implement right now.

You’re bound to come across content about ADHD, dyslexia, and other learning disabilities via your social scrolls and news push alerts, but you don’t have to take the hooks and headlines at their word.Instead, sign up for Understood News to stay informed of the latest developments without the fear-mongering headlines. You’ll get expert-reviewed updates on health, education policy, and topics related to neurodivergence.Maybe you’re trying to sort out the truth of whatever news has already come across your desk. It may help to scroll through Understood’s featured stories. There, you’ll find helpful articles like Are ADHD medications overprescribed in kids?, and Does [Acetaminophen] cause ADHD, autism, and other neurodevelopmental disorders?You can also stay up to date on the latest news by following Understood on Instagram and TikTok.

An individualized education program (IEP) is a formal plan created to help your kiddo do their best work at school with the help of staff support and services. Each IEP is designed for the individual child. For example, if your child has dyslexia, that IEP might include things like specialized reading lessons a few times a week.

While these programs are common (1 in 6 public school students use them), you may have lots of questions when entering that system for the first time. That’s where Understood’s “IEP Guide for Parents" can come in handy. The guide walks you through the basics, so you feel more prepared before you begin the process.

Even if you’re familiar with that system, recent news about changes to the Department of Education may make you wonder if your kid will still get the support they need, or what you can do if they don’t. Understood has a new investigative podcast — Zero Reject: The Uncertain Future of Special Education — which breaks down what’s changing and what’s at stake, and and lets parents know that they're not alone with the challenges they face.

Searching the internet blindly in 2026 can be completely overwhelming. The AI results with sketchy sourcing and the message board threads no one asked for are enough to make you give up before you even get started.

Instead of relying on your browser or AI apps, try using Understood’s AI-powered tool, the Understood Assistant, to dig in. The Assistant’s responses come from the extensive library of Understood's expert-reviewed content and nowhere else; no research hallucinations here.

When a child navigates the world differently, it can be hard to understand what they’re going through. Understood’s Through My Eyes is a free, immersive digital experience that lets you step into their world and experience their daily challenges firsthand. Through simulations and stories, it shows what a typical day can be like for kids with ADHD, dyslexia, and dyscalculia. It also offers videos and downloadable resources to help you support them. No matter where you and your kid are on your journey, you need real resources to help you navigate it. Start at Understood.org.

#61. I’m ashamed to admit I gatekeep my babysitter’s info

I know I'm not the only one. But I think it says more about what moms need than who they are.

By Katherine Rose Woller Updated Oct. 08, 2026

I opened my messages and read one simple text that instantly made me shudder.

“Does anyone have a sitter who is looking for a few extra hours?”

I stared at the mom-group thread on my phone, paralyzed by indecision. Caught somewhere between genuinely wanting to be helpful and quietly pretending I never saw the message in the first place. I’ll admit I went with the latter, uttered “yeaaaa no” under my breath, and gently placed my phone back on the table as I watched the text go unanswered.

You know we all read it, but not one mom responded that day.

No, I never replied. But yes, I felt bad, and I couldn’t push the nagging thoughts away. I was gatekeeping my babysitter.

I spent days wondering what this said about me. Did becoming a mom turn me into a selfish friend? That’s so far from who I strive to be. So far from how I typically try to show up in the world, and the opposite of what I want to model for my daughters. That was a tough pill to swallow.

Then, I wondered what this said about our community as a whole.

I always thought an integral part of friendship and community was sharing. Sharing stories, sharing the load, sharing resources. And honestly, that’s what moms do best. I’m amazed on an almost daily basis at how women support each other through every phase of womanhood.

But sharing caregivers? That’s where things get a bit more complicated.

Because to me, childcare isn’t just childcare.

It’s workouts, and doctor’s appointments, and yes, three hours in the salon chair so my colorist can work her magic.

It’s time to be Katherine, instead of just Mom.

Like many moms, I live in a suburb where even the college gals from the local university charge $25 an hour and have multiple offers on the table the second their info lands in a group chat.

No wonder I waffled when someone asked me to share the person who makes my life exponentially more manageable. Because it wasn’t that I didn’t want another couple to have a fabulous and probably long-overdue date night; I desperately want that for all my girlfriends. I just didn’t want their night out to come at the expense of my own much-needed respite. I was clinging to my one saving grace amongst a broader system that flat-out doesn’t support moms.

We were probably all having some version of the same internal debate, and our collective silence spoke volumes.

Scared that it might not be just a few extra hours here and there. Scared that our sitter might like the other family better. Scared things might get a little too serious for our liking. Scared we would lose our lifeline in surviving modern motherhood.

We were all just trying our best to carve out a life in a system that wasn’t built for thriving. Wasn’t built for identity outside of motherhood, or even a functional identity within it, for that matter. We all wanted to protect our sanity when, ironically, if we all shared just a bit more, we might not feel the scarcity as much in the first place.

I recently brought this topic to a Sunday morning moms’ yoga meet-up, and when I asked what the others thought of my reluctance to respond to the opening text, opinions were mixed.

Some were equally as protective; some shared cautiously. One mom even promised not to poach them if we would all please just share our sitters a time or two.

Bottom line, we all had our own invisible rules for managing and maintaining the support we undeniably needed. We had to.

On another day, in another text thread not so far away, I finally shared my babysitter’s info with a friend.

It allowed her and her husband to attend a concert they’d been eagerly awaiting for months. It gave our sitter the extra hours she was looking for, and it genuinely made me feel good to do a kindness for someone else.

Everyone won, and not at the expense of another.

Maybe motherhood didn’t make us all less generous after all. Maybe it just underlined how rare and precious support has become.

And maybe that’s exactly what every mom in my group chat was trying to protect.

#62. The Awkward Truth About Gym Class

Pretend you’re a tree. This was my earliest memory of physical education: our teacher, a tall and thin woman whose broad nimbus of dark hair was edged with gray, asking us to make-believe. By, as I understood it, not moving. In gym class. I was in second grade, and I was already confused. Somewhere here in my elementary school’s wood-floored gymnasium, I knew, there were ropes to climb, mats to tumble on, balls to kick and throw and dodge. And yet we were being corralled into this dumbed-down modern dance — the kind of hippie sh*t, I would later understand, that was typical of our Western Massachusetts college town.

Not that I was craving, or ever did crave, a traditional gym class. I was not made for gym. I was small — perpetually the second shortest boy in my grade — and slight and uninterested in the big sports that make up the bulk of public-school gym. I did not own a catcher’s mitt; no sane, responsible adult would let this shrimp play football.

At the same time, I was physical. I was a kid, after all. I wanted to run around, try a handstand, lift a dumbbell, shoot a basket, make a goal. And as uncoordinated and unenthusiastic as I was, I was not entirely untalented. I remember running a seven-minute mile in fourth grade. I could touch my toes and put one foot behind my head. My friend Jason and I competed to see who would be the first to knock out 60 sit-ups in a minute. I don’t remember who won.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class.

Those achievements and activities, however, had nothing to do with gym class as I experienced it. In the same way that English class was not designed to make philistines love literature, or biology to inspire dedication to the scientific method, gym class was not about converting us into athletes. Instead, it was a class for the kids who already were athletes, who played baseball and field hockey for fun, who owned weight machines at home, who didn’t need to sit through the gym teacher’s confounding explanation of what it meant to be “offsides.” I didn’t begrudge them their special class. I could spell and do algebra. They could throw an arcing spiral. This was the way of the world, even in a Massachusetts town full of ex-hippies.

And that all would have been just fine — if gym class had stuck with the most mainstream of sports. I could suck at soccer and blow at basketball, because who cared? Instead, gym class branched out, and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Swimming was a particular source of trauma. When I was 8, during a year my family spent living in Brighton, England, I was so tearfully reluctant to get in the pool that the headmaster of the school had to personally throw me in. And as I got older, the trauma morphed: Back in Massachusetts, the locker room after eighth-grade swimming lessons was a horror movie — I, the underdeveloped shrimp, had to undress surrounded by my Sasquatchian contemporaries. I have a memory of once changing entirely inside a locker, but that can’t be real. Those things were barely 10 inches wide. But another memory is definitely real: During one class, I dived into the deep end — and the force of the water as I entered yanked my swimsuit to my ankles. I don’t know how I had the wherewithal to pull them up before surfacing, but I did. I guess I was learning something.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class. Already awkward around girls, not to mention the implied romance of ballroom dance, I had the misfortune to be paired with Turtle Butt. Who was Turtle Butt? I don’t know. She was a girl I’d never spoken to, but one of my good friends had decided to call her Turtle Butt, even though, as far as I could tell, her butt did not resemble a turtle. And I was going to have to dance with her! Oh, the humiliation!

Gym class has always branched out from mainstream sports — and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Nearly 40 years later, I can now acknowledge that the humiliation was solely in my own head. I remember the potential embarrassment with infinitely more clarity than I remember any actual jeers or taunts, because there were none. But such is the world of the adolescent, where fears and anxieties dwarf reality.

And what I feared most of all was being seen. In other classes this didn’t happen. You might know where the Mason-Dixon Line was — or not. You might know how to deploy the quadratic formula — or not. Either way, you were not exposing anything about yourself other than your intellectual ability, or lack thereof.

It was similar in gym class. We all knew that some kids had it and some didn’t, and there was no shame in being terrible. (Asthma reduced my mile time to 20 minutes by eighth grade. But so what?) The difference, however, was that in gym class, unlike in history or math, you were a physical being. Strip away your ability to perform, and there you still stood, surrounded by your classmates, in sneakers and sweats or the jeans and T-shirt you wore to school that morning. You could pretend you’re a tree all you want — you remained visible: your prepubescent stature, your hairless lack of muscle tone, your terrapin posterior. There were no desks to hide behind, no escape from their eyes and their judgment.

No escape — except, perhaps, to grow up a little. In high school, my family moved to Southeastern Virginia, a place you’d think would have a sports and gym-class culture more extreme than that of the academic Yankees. Instead, gym was even more of an afterthought, not even required after sophomore or maybe junior year. Just like in second grade, I was confused. The school was full of jocks — guys who played soccer and football, girls on the field hockey team — and yet gym class was lackadaisical at best. Driver’s ed occupied a couple of months of the curriculum, and on Fridays, we’d ride a school bus to a nearby bowling alley, where nerds like me, who had no hope of throwing a strike, could at least show off by knowing how to score the game correctly.

Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not.

In fact, I considered the bowling alley my place — because I was there all the time, after school. Technically, not in the bowling alley, but just outside, where almost every day I would meet my skateboarder friends to ride the concrete drainage ditch next to its parking lot. In high school, skating had become my life, my all-consuming hobby, my… my… sport? Yes, my sport! After having failed at all of the mainstream sports, I’d finally found this one sweaty, filthy, wonderful way to be an athlete (though I would never have used that word back then). And while I wasn’t pro material, I wasn’t too bad at it, either. I could hold my own among my friends, at competitions in Virginia Beach, on road trips to Richmond and Washington, D.C. And more important, I could do so without fretting about being seen, in some unspeakable way, by the kids around me. Skateboarding required us to accept one another, in all our foibles and weirdnesses. Because if we didn’t, then who would we skate with?

I stuck with skateboarding for most of a decade, before aging out postcollege and taking up distance running and, more recently, rock climbing. As with skateboarding, I’m pretty good at both, if not truly exceptional, and I appreciate the physical experience of each in ways I could not have imagined in high school. At times, I’ve wondered: If gym class had taught us how to run, or how to scale a boulder, would I have discovered and loved those sports decades earlier? Somehow, I doubt it. Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not. What mattered was what happened after school, in every sense of the term. Still, gym class did teach me this one important lesson about public education: If you make like a tree, you can leave.

#65. Things My Kids Do Right Now That I Never Want to Forget

When I hear her yell “starfish” from the other side of the door, that’s my cue to start the music. It could be “Problem” by Ariana Grande, Kelly Clarkson’s “Since U Been Gone,” or any other song from the & Juliet soundtrack (her first play ever). Then my wild-spirited six-year-old bursts through the door and does an improvised dance. Since she doesn’t take lessons, it’s always more Elaine Benes than Beyoncé, and it never gets old.

I’m very aware this won’t last forever. It’s one of the hundreds of phases my children will pass through that are joyful and hilarious and fleeting. The everyday moments that tell our family’s story so much better than the big milestones. The ones we share with our partners and best friends to make them laugh or drop tons of emojis.

Like when my son wrestles Carlton, his white stuffed bear. He’s in the thick of a WWE obsession, learning every wrestler’s name, personality, stats, and best moves, and he regularly subjects poor Carlton to Stone Cold Stunners and the odd German Suplex. It’s a solid part of his nine-year-old bedtime routine, and I’ve taken tons of videos from his doorway while “Macho Man Jr.” flexes his skills on a small stuffie.

As parents, our text chains and camera rolls are cluttered with these kinds of silly photos, videos, and anecdotes—but when nostalgia hits, we’re lucky if we can actually find them. I used to jot down the funny words that my kids would mispronounce for a few months (never correct them, because when they stop saying “kenks” instead of thanks, you’ll miss it) and the weird things they did in my notes app. But as they grow, I feel like I have less bandwidth for this kind of remembering.

In a panic over the thought of forgetting that my daughter says “potopoty” instead of apostrophe and my son calls a duvet a “dubet,” I started adding all these moments to a Tinybeans album called “Quirks.” I use the captions to tell the stories behind the photos and videos, and the new voice memos to record the mispronunciations or quickly dictate something they’ve been doing lately. They’re curated, organized, and easily shared with the grandparents, uncles and aunties, and my besties.

It’s where you’ll find photos of the little love notes and updates my daughter leaves on my work to-do lists: “love mom,” “I like being with you,” “mommy mi tooth fell out!!!” Or pictures of our latest learn-to-draw masterpieces, where she bossily guides me in drawing something totally offbeat in very specific ways. You’ll also hear about how my son still loves to watch the original Muppet Show, Dodo videos about dogs, and old black-and-white Mickey Mouse cartoons, and the particularly adorable way he looks when he groggily stumbles down the hall to the bathroom in the middle of the night and I’m lucky enough to be awake.

Some mysteries of childhood I’ll probably never solve, like how to get him to eat anything that isn’t beige or how to get her to stop swearing like a sailor. But I’ve figured out how to keep track of the rest of it, and my best advice is to find a great system to keep these moments close. Because you won’t know when it’s the last time they yell “starfish” and strut through the door, but you’re definitely going to want to relive it for years to come (one more for the Quirks album).

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#66. My Ex & I Have Better Sex Now That We’re Divorced Co-Parents

We were terrible married partners. Now, it seems to be working.

Welcome to Ask A MWLTF (Yes, that’s Mother Who Likes to F*ck.), a monthly anonymous advice column from Scary Mommy. Here we’ll dissect all your burning questions about motherhood, sex, romance, intimacy, and friendship with the help of our columnist, Penelope, a writer and mental health practitioner in training. She’ll dish out her most sound advice for parents on the delicate dance of raising kids without sacrificing other important relationships. Email her at askpenelope@scarymommy.com.

My ex-husband and I were terrible married partners. We fought constantly, divorced, and became surprisingly good co-parents. Now, years later, we’ve started sleeping together again. The weird thing is, the sex is better than it was when we were married. We’re more relaxed, more playful, and somehow more honest with each other. We can flirt and laugh and enjoy being together without falling into the same arguments that made our marriage miserable. We still have kids together, so we see each other all the time, and we’ve managed to build a pretty peaceful routine.

The only problem: I’m starting to worry that we’re going to ruin it. Neither of us want to get back together, and we’re not exactly dating. I don’t even know if he’s seeing other people. I also don’t know how I’d feel if he did. Part of me thinks this is a great arrangement: we know each other, we have history, and the sex is good. Another part of me wonders if we’re just reopening a door we worked really hard to close. How do I know if this is something we can enjoy without messing up the co-parenting relationship we finally got right?

There is a particular kind of romantic comedy that begins after the divorce. The marriage was a disaster, the couple finally separates, and then — once they’re no longer sharing a mortgage, a bathroom, and the exhausting daily business of being married —they discover that they actually like each other. Maybe they even have great sex. It’s a charming premise, in part because it seems to promise that the problem was never the two people themselves, but the institution of marriage, with its endless negotiations over money, chores, parenting, and whose turn it is to be disappointed.

Real life, of course, is not always so neatly plotted. But there is something psychologically plausible about the experience you describe. Marriage and co-parenting ask people to do different things. As spouses, you were entangled in the daily expectations of a shared life. You had to negotiate not just who you were to each other, but who would do what, who was letting whom down, whose needs took precedence, and what your family was supposed to look like. You may have been fighting about the dishes, but the argument was rarely only about the dishes. It was about whether you felt seen, whether you could count on each other, whether one of you was carrying too much, whether the other was asking too much. Over time, every small disagreement can become a referendum on the whole relationship.

Now you have a different arrangement. You each have your own home, your own routines, and some degree of control over your own lives. You can be attentive and affectionate during the time you choose to spend together, and then go home. You’re no longer trying to make every part of your lives fit together. It may be easier to be generous with each other when you’re not also negotiating the entire architecture of your family. Also, there’s another possible ingredient: distance can make room for curiosity. When you were married, you knew each other in the exhausting, unvarnished way people know someone they live with. You saw each other sick, irritated, distracted, and overwhelmed. You had to deal with the consequences of each other’s habits and choices every day. Now, even with children in common, you may be encountering each other in smaller, more deliberate doses. Your ex can be a person you’re attracted to again, rather than the person who forgot to sign the permission slip or left you to handle a family crisis alone. You can have a good evening without needing it to prove that your whole life together is working. That doesn’t mean the sex is fake, or that you’re necessarily fooling yourselves. It may be real pleasure, real affection, even a new kind of intimacy. But good sex can mean many things, and it doesn’t automatically mean that the conditions that made your marriage unhappy have changed. You may have become better at being co-parents, or better at being exes, without having become more compatible as spouses. Those are meaningful accomplishments in their own right. You don’t have to turn them into a reunion story.

The question I’d pay attention to isn’t just whether you can keep having sex without fighting. It’s what happens when the situation becomes less convenient or less clear. What if one of you starts dating someone else? What if one of you wants more commitment, or less? What if one of you begins to feel jealous, or hopes the sex means you’re getting back together, while the other sees it as a pleasurable arrangement with no larger implications? And what happens if the old arguments return — not over household chores, perhaps, but over the kids, the schedule, or the meaning of what you’re doing? Because your children are part of this, even if the sex itself is private. You don’t need to share adult details with them, and you certainly don’t need to explain your sex life. But if the renewed relationship starts to look like a reconciliation to them, or if it changes the emotional temperature between their parents, they may notice. Children can be hopeful about their parents getting back together, even when nobody has promised that. They can also feel unsettled if a warm, cooperative co-parenting relationship suddenly becomes tense again. Protecting them doesn’t require you to avoid intimacy with your ex at all costs. It does mean taking care not to let uncertainty between the two of you spill into the family’s routines without talking about it.

All that said I’d suggest having a conversation that may feel less sexy than the sex itself, but is probably more important. I’m not talking about a grand summit about the future of your relationship, nor a demand that either of you define what this means before you’re allowed to enjoy it. What I’m suggesting is more of an honest check-in: Are we both seeing this the same way? Are we free to date other people? What would we want to happen if one of us developed feelings or wanted to stop? What boundaries would help us preserve the co-parenting relationship we’ve worked so hard to build? And if you’re not sure of the answers yet, can you agree to say so honestly rather than letting the ambiguity quietly become a promise? You may discover that you both want the same thing: a sexual connection that feels good and familiar, without trying to rebuild the marriage. You may discover that one of you is hoping for more. Either way, it’s better to know what you’re each consenting to than to assume the arrangement means the same thing to both of you just because the sex is good.

Finally, you don’t have to treat the fact that you divorced as proof that you should never be together again. People change. Relationships change. Sometimes the end of a marriage creates the conditions for a more peaceful connection. But you also don’t have to treat good sex as evidence that you should give the marriage another try. Maybe what you’ve found is a way to enjoy a part of your history without repeating all of it.

#67. Coach Mando's Advice For Dads Coaching Youth Sports

Brendan Wayne, the man who is The Mandalorian, has been coaching youth sports for more than 20 years. Here’s his advice to other coaches and parents on the sidelines.

When you watch the hit Star Wars TV show The Mandalorian — or the new film The Mandalorian and Grogu — and you start to wonder if there’s something about being a bounty hunter with a heart of gold that can help you with youth sports, you’re not nuts. It’s possible that just through osmosis, thanks to the motions of Mando himself, you’re getting some good sense of how to be a better sports parent. Here’s why: The actor who has played the body of The Mandalorian since 2019, Brendan Wayne, has been coaching soccer for 23 years. In addition to starting a new podcast, Hats & Helmets, Wayne is currently the coach of the Lady Lancers soccer team at Grant High School in California.

“I’ve played sports my whole life,” Wayne tells Fatherly. “It’s one of the greatest things a kid can learn to do.”

As the summer starts to give way to the beginning of school, we reached out to Wayne to get his core principles as a longtime coach of youth sports. This man may know how to calm down Baby Yoda, but that’s just acting. As a soccer coach, Wayne is an even bigger expert. Here’s his clear advice for parents of sporty kids, youth coaches, and why athletics can be great for all kinds of kids.

Wayne’s core coaching philosophy isn’t focused on winning; instead, he feels the only thing that makes a team is the notion of togetherness.

Many parents have been there. The game is going a certain way, and you can’t help yourself with your thoughts. You’ve shouted out something; you’ve even has words with a ref or the coach. What should you do? Wayne’s feelings are very, very clear.

Even as a coach, Wayne doesn’t shout at his players while the game is actually happening. The coaching comes before the game happens, not from the sidelines.

Sometimes, a kid can lose interest in their sport. Or maybe they’re feeling like they’re not part of the team. What can coaches and sports parents do? For Wayne, it’s not about quitting right away but about looking at athletics more holistically.

As an actor and performer, Wayne knows a thing or two about how to keep all aspects of his body in shape — fitting into that Mandalorian armor doesn’t just happen by accident. One of his biggest beliefs, which he applies to youth sports, is that a person has to look at the big picture. For Wayne, it’s all about making sure kids are getting different kinds of exercises.

If you do need to say something to a kid who looks frustrated out there in the game, keep in mind that most of these kids aren’t going pro. Some might, but that’s not the point of this moment.

When Wayne sees one of his kids on the field and they need inspiration, he sometimes just tries to lighten the moment.

#68. The Cornell 7 and raising boys in a world filled with casual cruelty

The bar is higher now. We must teach our sons what real courage means in a culture that continues to demean women.

By Neha Gandhi Updated Oct. 02, 2026

At this point, tens of thousands of words have been spilled about the Cornell 7, the group of seven fraternity brothers at Cornell University accused of drugging and sexually assaulting a 20-year-old student over the course of seven hours in 2024. There’s outrage at the legal system that failed Jane Doe; there’s disgust with the power structures that allow some families and some men to face limited consequences for their actions; there’s a rallying cry to ban frats on campuses.

And then, there are all of the moms out there, at a loss for how to raise boys who don’t hurt women—and don’t stand by quietly when other people hurt women. Tomika Anderson wrote in Essence this week: “ I want to raise a son who understands that his responsibility to another human being doesn’t end with, I didn’t do it.”

Because it defies reason, right? How are we raising young men who, en masse, are comfortable referring to a drugged and incapacitated woman as sexually available in the crudest terms possible? Men who use phrases like, “shop still open?” to find out if they too can participate in her alleged gang rape? How is it possible that not one single student in the seemingly fraternity-wide group chat titled “Chi Phi Actives”  alerted the authorities when that text went out?

It’s actually not that surprising; in fact, it’s the probable outcome of the systems that we have collectively built. The small gains we might have made over the years, in accountability for sexual violence, some movement toward gender equity, and in bodily autonomy, are slipping away. And they’re being replaced by casual violence, sexism, and normalized cruelty—all rewarded by algorithms that value reaction above all else.

That idea of normalizing cruelty is what guts me — as a woman, as a human, as a parent.

Because it’s hard to imagine that those seven frat boys at Cornell came to their casual cruelty through a lack of choice and opportunity. They were at one of the best schools in the country—they had all the choices in the world and all of the opportunities ahead of them.

What’s alleged in Jane Doe’s lawsuit could only have taken place if the men she named had a casual disregard for her life, body, and autonomy. If they didn’t see her as equally human. If perhaps, they didn’t see her at all. We’ve heard so many times that rape isn’t about sex. It’s about power. These men allegedly exercised their power over a drugged and incapacitated 20-year-old. Eventually, two of them, by Doe’s account, intervened to “shut it down.” But not before seven alleged assaults. Not a single boy in the group chat was willing to give up whatever modicum of power and status he had within the group to speak up before the assaults happened, or call the police, or to remind the rest of the group of this woman’s humanity. Let alone to help her leave the house.

The internet is ablaze with women shouting for justice, for accountability, and for change. And for raising boys who know and do better. How do we ensure our boys don’t morph from sweet, kind, good boys into monsters — without our clocking it?

My own son is fortunate enough to attend an elementary school where the educators and administrators spend a lot of time thinking about how we educate young boys — both so we don’t leave them behind, and so we celebrate and elevate what is special about them. What’s interesting to me is that the divide between boys and girls becomes so clear during these years. Speaking in generalizations, boys wiggle and have difficulties with impulse control. Girls activate the communication centers of their brains much earlier on and clearly and easily raise their hands, do “whole-body listening,” and verbalize their thoughts and ideas.

From the perspective of my 1st grader, who has traditionally gravitated towards close friendships with girls, “girls are better at everything.” And I can see that he feels his own sense of inequity in this. Things are often easier for girls. Their brains develop differently. And sometimes, they are even unkind about it, and his sensitive soul explodes with the injustice of it all.

But it’s my job — perhaps my main job, after keeping him safe and fed and sheltered — to start to bring context to his feelings. I can’t allow this feeling of competitiveness or inequity to shape his view of how men and women should treat each other. I can’t let it plant the seeds of resentment toward girls and women. In the closed bubble of elementary school, perhaps girls have an unfair advantage. But out in the world writ large, the decks are stacked against us.

I’m starting to have some of these conversations with him now — not sharing the deepest depths of darkness out there, but using his obsession with Hamilton or his interest in Greek mythology to point out the power structures limiting Angelica Schuyler or Penelope or Eurydice from living life on their own terms. (Shout out to the Greeking Out podcast from National Geographic—their “oracle” interjects with asides observing sexism, racism, and other problematic behaviors in the most kid-friendly way.)

But even more urgently, I see now that I have to talk to him about cruelty. We are making our way through the second Harry Potter book at present, and there are some teachable moments in there. The word “mudblood,” the treatment of Dobby the house elf, and Draco Malfoy’s reflections of his dad’s biases have been particularly fertile ground for discussion.

But just as we talk about inclusion — “If someone says you can play but your friend can’t, you have to just say ‘that’s not cool,’ and find something else to play. Because we take care of our friends and are kind to everyone” — we also have to start talking about cruelty. What it might look like, why it might be confusing to spot when others disguise in a veneer of casual fun, and how to tell others to stop — or at least walk away and find a trusted adult who can intervene.

This last part is essential, because group dynamic peer pressure is particularly powerful in boys, and it’s not enough to raise kids who know what the right choice is and can make it for themselves.

We need our kids to be active participants in this world who speak their minds when they see others doing something wrong, even when the consequence might be ridicule and social isolation.

Before I had kids, I would have assumed that if you inculcate your kids with a clear idea of right and wrong, and a strong sense of their own values, nothing like this could happen. But now I’m not so sure. I know for a fact that it’s not good enough to just lead by example. Don’t get me wrong: That part is important. But we also have to have hard conversations, and be honest about this world and its realities so our kids don’t come face to face with hard things unarmed with anything more than a Pollyannaish sense of good and evil.

Our culture, our political leaders, and our media are filled with ideas about casual racism, sexism, bigotry, and cruelty. The internet is vast and full of rabbit holes waiting to radicalize our boys, if we aren’t vigilant. And the power of a persuasive group of peers to a kid with a partially developed prefrontal cortex and a desire to fit in is unfathomably strong. So, I have to arm my kid with something even stronger than that.

I have to teach him about the specific cruelties of this world. I have to give him (age-appropriate) context. And I have to have deeply uncomfortable conversations early and often. I also have to recruit my husband into these efforts. And as I think about that piece of the puzzle, I’m deeply grateful to be married to someone I feel entirely values-aligned with. Someone who doesn’t casually disrespect waitresses or make off-color comments about actresses’ bodies. Someone who doesn’t have to put on a show of respecting women because he inherently does. But I also have to persuade him to be more vocal about what happens in gendered spaces from a place of authority, because I know at some point, my kid’s going to start to tune me out and say, “Mom, you just don’t get it.”

And as I look around at what’s happening in this world, I really don’t get it.
