#125. Why The First Animated 'Hobbit' Is Good For Your Kids

In 1977, the animated version of The Hobbit made a classic book even more powerful than ever.

Back on November 27, 1977, kids watching network TV were introduced to the “greatest adventure” of all time. Although the original Star Wars blew everyone’s minds that summer and forever altered the way we think about blockbuster movies, the Jules Bass and Arthur Rankin Jr. version of The Hobbit quietly pushed the most famous fantasy origin story of all into the mainstream. 45 years later, the impact of the animated Hobbit cannot be overstated.

Clocking at just 77 minutes (and apparently, not an hour and a half as many remember it), the animated version of The Hobbit from Rankin and Bass captures the breezy and jaunty quality of J.R.R. Tolkien’s 1937 children’s novel The Hobbit. Of course, even by 1977, The Hobbit had been retroactively relegated to “prequel” status, making it something of an underdog next to the sprawling, and mega-popular Lord of the Rings trilogy of novels, which had been published, originally from 1954 to 1955. Before this, in 1951, Tolkien had revised The Hobbit, to make it more closely aligned with the spirit of The Lord of the Rings, making the slightly more childish version of the book a historical memory.

Bilbo Baggins (Orson Bean) and Gollum (Theodore Isidore Gottlieb) in 'The Hobbit.'

However, the 1977 animated Hobbit, firmly took the world of Middle-earth and made the adventure for children. With their experiences on other animated kids’ specials like Frosty the Snowman, Rankin and Bass upped their game significantly for The Hobbit, mostly because they had amazing source material to work with. While hardcore Tolkien heads are very aware of the various songs throughout the book versions of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, for the casual viewer in 1977, the staggering amount of music in the animated Hobbit might have seemed weird. However, it was Jules Bass himself who adapted a good chunk of Tolkien’s lyrics directly from the book and then assisted composer Maury Laws, in making it all happen.

The famous Glenn Yarbrough-sung folksy ballad, “The Greatest Adventure,” was, in fact, the only song that was original to the movie, and not derived from the pages of The Hobbit. This single fact is the microcosm that demonstrates the overall brilliance of this version of The Hobbit; it’s both wildly faithful to the source material, but also morphs into a significantly separate adaptation. Just as Bilbo’s stories of his meeting with Gollum later turned out to be unreliable, the 1977 Hobbit succeeded in turning Tolkien’s book into a modern folk tale. Depending on who was retelling the story, the story could change. Before 1977, this hadn’t happened yet with The Hobbit, and other than Tolkien’s revisions, alternate versions of the story simply couldn’t exist.

As scholars and students of folk tales and fairy tales will tell you; what ensures that a story survives isn’t just the preservation of the text, but instead, the retellings of a story is what creates immortality. In the time before the printed word, this was accomplished through the oral tradition, but in the late 20th century, film adaptations began to do something similar.

With its unforgettable animation style, brilliant pacing, hilarious moments, excellent casting, and yes, whimsically endearing music, The Hobbit was the first of its kind: A new take on what had already been an instant classic in 1937. Like the film version of The Wizard of Oz, the 1977 Hobbit sublimated a wonderful kids’ book into a brilliant piece of modern animation. Today, we might think of the 1977 Hobbit as retro. But the reason why it was so important is that, when it comes to amazing fantasy adaptions, the future began right here.

You can rent The Hobbit on Amazon Prime Video right here. It is also included in Fatherly’s 100 Best Kids Movies Ever.

#126. 35 Gravestone Baby Names Borrowed From Historical Headstones

For some of us, spending time in cemeteries is a routine thing. And while you might enjoy the walking paths and the easy escape from daily conversations, there’s something else lurking among the headstones. I’m not talking about ghosts, although there might be ghosts. I’m referring to gravestone-inspired baby names.

Graveyards can provide endless inspiration for potential names for your future baby, invoking forgotten vintage names and unique spellings. In fact, earlier this year, one family went viral for strolling around their local cemetery in search of the perfect name for their newest addition. To see just how rich the naming inspo at graveyards is, a few Scary Mommy editors and I went to burial plots near us, including a few in the historic cities of Salem, Massachusetts; Charleston, South Carolina; and Savannah, Georgia. We found some serious gems, and wouldn’t using one be a nice nod to those who carried the names before?

So, if you’re looking for a name that honors the dead and celebrates the living, check out these 29 unexpected and charming baby names taken from actual headstones.

A name with Hebrew roots, Asa means “healer” or “doctor.” Captain Asa Hooper was a notable sea captain and privateer in the 18th century around Marblehead, Massachusetts, so this is a great name if you want a kind, sea-loving child.

This name with Ecclesiastical roots means “father” or “priest,” and belonged to one Abbott Hall Brisbane — a brigadier general who now lies in Accabee Plantation Cemetery in Summerville, South Carolina. Born in 1804, Brisbane seems to have lived an interesting and illustrious life: a West Point graduate, a decorated military officer, a superintendent for the Charleston and Cincinnati Railroad, and a history professor at Charleston’s esteemed military academy, The Citadel. So, perhaps a name of acclaim?

Scandinavian in origin, the name Iver is sometimes spelled Ivarr or Ivarrs. It comes from the Norse word for yew tree. Because bows of warriors were often made from the sacred yew, the name Iver means “warrior” or “bow warrior.” Totally up to you if you want to pronounce it like the singer Bon Iver (ee-vare).

An alternative to Colette or Nicolette, this French-inspired name means “victorious people” or “victory of the people.” A perfect name for a future Justice of the Peace, world leader, or class president.

A version of the more common name William or Wilhelmina, Wilmot means “protection”. Sadly, this name did not protect Wilmot Redd, who was one of the many innocent victims of the Salem Witch Trials (and the only woman accused of witchcraft in neighboring Marblehead, Massachusetts, to be hanged during the trials).

Looking for a fresh alternative to Leo? This gender-neutral name comes from the word lion or leon and means “little lion.”

A divine name, Celestine is a unique version of the beautiful name Celeste. It means “of the stars” or “heavenly,” being derived from the Latin word for heaven, caelestis or caleum.

Artemus is considered a gender-neutral spelling of its namesake, Artemis, the Greek goddess of the wild hunt. No matter how you spell it, the name connotes fierceness and warrior energy.

More frequently spelled as Vercie, this name comes from the French word verce, which means “truth” or “truthfulness.”

Agnes has its roots in the Greek language and means “pure, chaste, or holy.” You can call them Aggie or the less-common name Nes, for short.

The name Chillian is a less common spelling of the name Cillian, an Irish name that translates roughly to “little church.” Though the “h” may be silent, the kid is sure to be chill. Variations include Cilian, Kilian, and Gillian.

Milda is the Lithuanian Goddess of Love, and the name is derived from the Lithuanian word for gracious. A child gifted with this name will surely be a blessing, invoking love, passion, and true grace.

Discovered on a moss-covered gravestone at Allen AME Church Cemetery on Edisto Island, South Carolina, this name combines the classic and feminine “Eve” with more melodic names such as Helena. According to Nameberry, it’s relatively uncommon but has popped up sporadically in records dating back to the 19th century (which makes sense, as this Evelena was born just after, in 1918).

This once-popular early 19th century name doesn’t surface as much anymore. It has Latin origins as Albinus and the variations Albin, Albe, and Albie are used more commonly in Sweden and France. The name means “white, bright, or fair.”

Conrad Aiken was a Pulitzer Prize-winning poet, writer, and editor. It is said Aiken wanted his grave in Savannah’s Bonaventure Cemetery to have a bench so that poetry lovers could sit and drink with him in the afterlife. (Fun fact: His grave gained notoriety after being mentioned in John Berendt's book Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil.) The name Conrad is of both Old English and Old German origins and translates to “bold counsel.” Aiken would also make a perfect name for a little writer-to-be, FWIW.

A name of Greek and Latin origin, the name Eusebe is a rarer form of the more common name Eusebia, Eusebius, or Eusebio. The name means “devout” and is based on both a Biblical and early Greek philosophical concept of exemplifying godliness and piety.

Want to imbue your kid with strength of character and integrity? Buried in Magnolia Cemetery, Burnet Rhett Maybank was the mayor of Charleston, a U.S. Senator, and the 99th governor of South Carolina. During his tenure as governor in the late 1930s, he publicly fought against the Ku Klux Klan and worked to improve underserved Black schools. The name Burnet or Burnett means brown-haired. Rhett, which means “counselor” or “advisor,” is a charming name, too.

If you love the idea of a traditional name, consider Abigail. This sweet option means “my father’s joy.” But be forewarned: it’s definitely a popular pick, so your kid will be one of many.

Not only does it invoke our favorite Mistress of the Dark, Elvira is a name with deeper meaning as well. Some translations declare it to mean “happiness,” and others say the name invokes the words “truth or spear,” as in the spear of justice.

There are only two words on the gravestone of Maybell Lafayette, who lies in rest at Allen AME Church Cemetery just outside Charleston, South Carolina: “loving mother.” And what a beautiful thing to mark one’s life! This sweet-as-can-be name means “lovable” or “dear.”

A masculine variant of Emily, both names are derived from the Roman Aemilia or Amelia. Depending on who you ask, the name can either connote striving and excelling, eagerness, or it translates simply to “rival.”

Delina, a Sicilian derivative of Adelina and Adeline, means “grace” and “noble one.” In Tigrinya, a dialect of Ethiopia, the word “delina” means to desire or want.

Mercer derives from the French word merce for merchant, so the name is sometimes translated as “shopkeeper” or “vendor.” The Italian translation is similar, with merce meaning goods or wares for sale. John Mercer was a renowned musician who co-founded Capitol Records and was laid to rest in death at Savannah’s Bonaventure Cemetery.

This imperial girl’s name was common among royal families and gained popularity during the Victorian era, especially for eighth children. Why? Because Octavia means “eighth,” of course! It’s unclear whether Octavia A. Bart was an eighth child. Her gravestone tells us only that she was a native of Boulogne-sur-Mer, France, who departed this life Aug. 19, 1871, at 18 years old, and rests in peace at the Circular Congregational Church Burying Ground in historic Charleston, South Carolina.

Want to try to lay the groundwork for an agreeable child? Name them Evarist. Based on the Latin evaristus, this name translates to “agreeable or well-pleasing.” Other variations of this name include the Spanish Evaristo and the French Evariste. It can be pronounced “Ava-rist” or “Ev-a-rist.”

A popular, gender-neutral name, Francis means “Frenchman” or “free man.” Francis Girdler, whose grave is pictured here, has an interesting tie-in to Salem history. Before his death, he was married to Deborah Girdler, who went on to marry Ambrose Gale — a man who famously testified against Wilmot Redd, the only Marblehead woman to be hanged for witchcraft in 1692.

It will come as no surprise that this charming name means “made of gold.” Sometimes. Used as a shortened form of Golda, you could do worse than liken your child to a precious metal or a beloved actress (Goldie Hawn).

Tragically, a young man named Maxwell Campbell, alongside his brother Henry, died of consumption in 1851. He was only 25, and his gravestone was erected by his “bereaved mother.” We know nothing else of Maxwell (or Henry, for that matter), aside from the fact that their lives were cut short. But perhaps he lives on in perpetuity through those who share his Scottish name, which means “Mack’s stream.”

Little Gracie Watson is the most famous resident of Bonaventure Cemetery in Savannah, Georgia. The young girl died of pneumonia in 1889, and her ghost is said to haunt the cemetery to this day. The name Grace or Gracie means a blessing, derived from the word gratia in Latin, where we also get the word gratitude.

Can’t say we’ve heard this name before, making it an ideal choice if you’re looking for something super unique! This Doddridge was born in 1768 in Massachusetts and, upon his passing in 1847, was buried at the Circular Congregational Church in Charleston, South Carolina, beside an Eliza with the same last name, who we can only assume was his wife. According to Ancestry.com, Doddridge is an English habitational name.

Want a baby goth in the house? The name Gotha is derived from Goth, and is more commonly seen as a surname. The meaning is “tribe” or “clan.” Gotha is also a city in Germany whose name in High German translates to “good waters.”

One of the oldest forms of the name Mary, this name’s alternate spellings include Mirriam. The name is believed to be of Hebrew origin and has several possible meanings. The most inspiring one is “of the sea” or “star of the sea,” which invokes a mermaidian feel. Other meanings include “beloved” and “bitterness.”

A once common name in Ancient Rome, the name Lavina literally means “woman of Rome.” This name gives off major girl-boss vibes and connotes strength. I also adore the name Clarice, which means “clarity” or “brightness.”

Zadok is an underused and intriguing Hebrew name that means “just” and “righteous.” (Zadok, who died in 1836 and sleeps eternally in the Circular Congregational Church Burying Ground of Charleston, bears the last name Jesup... which would also be a cool name.)

This classic, gender-neutral name of Latin origin means “wise,” “skilled,” or “intelligent.” Although it has tapered off dramatically in popularity since the Middle Ages, it’s seeing a resurgence thanks to TV mentions (Prudence Featherington, anyone?). Plus, the nickname “Pru” is so cute.

#127. The Best Back-to-School TV Episodes For Every Age

Timeless back-to-school episodes for kids, from toddlerhood through high school.

All good things must come to an end, or so the saying goes, and when you’re a kid that’s never more true than when late August rolls around and summer vacation draws to a close. Going back to school means an end to unscheduled days of fun in the sun, but it can also be the start of something good. The first day of school can be the first time a kid meets their new best friend, or it can kick off an important semester of learning and discovery. It can also be, well, not so good. Sometimes, back-to-school is hard.

This is why families sometimes turn to our greatest TV shows for guidance. TV isn’t the perfect teacher, but it can help families reflect on their own experiences in cathartic ways. Here are 10 of the best back-to-school episodes, an assortment that captures the highs and lows of stepping back into the classroom — or stepping into a new one for the first time. These episodes are listed here roughly in how young the target audience is for each. So, we’ll start with toddlers and end with high schoolers!

As one might expect from a series based on Mr. Rogers’ Neighborhood, “A Visit to School” showcases the same gentle understanding and straightforward communication the beloved children’s show host excelled at. If you’re feeling scared about doing something new — like going to the first day of school — talking it out and preparing for the new experience is a great way to feel more confident. It’s actionable advice.

These two Arthur episodes, from the very start and very end of the long-running PBS series, show how every back-to-school comes with its own challenges — and how all of them can be overcome. In the first episode, Arthur and Buster are nervous about their new third-grade teacher, Mr. Ratburn, until they learn he’s not actually scary at all. Then, 15 real years later, Arthur’s excited to be moving on to 4th grade, until he realizes his best friend Buster won’t be in his class anymore. But, that doesn’t mean that they’ll stop being friends.

The Disney Channel series Recess is focused on a group of elementary school friends, but not every member of “the gang” was in the first episode. It’s not until the second episode that Gus Griswald shows up at school. Recess has a great way of heightening normal playground politics and Gus’ struggle to escape the “new kid” label is one that anybody who has transferred schools probably empathizes with — and there’s a very happy ending. Not only does Gus get his actual name back and ditch the “new kid” moniker, but he also gets a group of fast friends.

The first episode of the Netflix kids' show Karma’s World has the titular character excited about her first day of middle school, only to initially be met with a bully who makes fun of her name Things end up all right, as she makes a friend and the bully eventually apologizes, and the episode offers a more representational take of the back-to-school story.

DJ Tanner’s first day of junior high does not go well, and not just because she’s accidentally dressed just like her teacher, which is just about the least cool thing you can do. She’s also feeling less developed than her classmates, and she only has one class with her friend Kimmy. But, “Back to School Blues” knows that a first day of school is always followed by a second day of school, and DJ (with some guidance for Danny) returns the next day with a good attitude and a little more age-appropriate outfit.

Cory and Shawn’s first day of school is exactly as melodramatic as you’d expect from Boy Meets World, but’s also a pretty heavy look at bullying and brotherly bonds, as Eric stands up for his younger bro even though the “cool” politics of having a younger sibling in the same school as you are fraught, at best. And, Boy Meets World gets to keep the sitcom status quo while also shaking things up with the reveal that Mr. Feely has been promoted to be the principal of their new school.

Most back-to-school episodes are focused, understandably, on the kids who are stepping back into the classroom. But, it’s a big day for parents, too, and this Season 5 episode of Modern Family focuses more on parents Phil and Gloria as they come to grips with the fact that Luke and Manny are growing up!

OK, chances are the average student doesn’t need to list “vampires” as one of their concerns on the first day of school. But, even if Buffy the Vampire Slayer’s premiere episode isn’t as relatable as some of the other entries on this list, it’s still a great back-to-school episode. Sometimes school sucks, and sometimes it sucks blood.

#128. Danielle Fishel Is Just As You Expect Her To Be

The Boy Meets World and Dancing With The Stars alum opens up to Scary Mommy about parenting, her wellness journey, and who she’s rooting for on DWTS.

I’m 44, and like so many others my age, I spent my Friday nights (and let’s be honest, Saturday mornings) glued to ABC and NBC watching teen-based sitcoms. Boy Meets World was, of course, one of those shows, and one of my favorites. So when I got a chance to talk to Danielle Fishel, aka Topanga herself, I nearly peed my pants.

Like me, Fishel is now also a mom to two sports-loving sons, ages 7 and 5. And like 1.9 million other people, I follow her on Instagram to get a dose of nostalgia, a heap of funny motherhood moments, and so much more. I caught up with the actor and mom via Zoom, and suffice it to say, I had a blast. We talked about our matching Stanleys (hers filled with Metamucil fiber powder, mine with protein powder because #agingmillennials), motherhood, and what her post-cancer life looks like now.

Scary Mommy: Let’s jump right in. What's your wellness like now as a mid-40s lady?

Danielle Fishel: My wellness routine now, in my mid-40s, is very clear to me. I used to just kind of, like, waffle in and out of different trends, and now I really know what works for me, and I just prioritize it. And a lot of that's even just stuff I've learned in the last year or two. But my wellness routine really begins with the way I start my day every single day, which is waking up at least 30 minutes before my kids, because I have to have some coffee and some silence before I start my day.

DF: Somewhere between 5:30 and 6. I get up every day, and I need to start my morning with that quiet time. And actually before I even get to my coffee, the very first thing I do is I start my day with fiber. And my medications that I take. I really just started myself on my health journey. I include fiber right from the beginning of my day because, as a type A personality, I like to wake up and already start checking things off my list.

SM: I understand that. It’s like, look what I've already done!

DF: Yeah, look at what I've already done, and I haven't even had a cup of coffee yet. So that makes me feel good. The quiet time before my kids get up helps me start my day mentally, and then working out is extremely important to me as part of my wellness journey. It’s become a lot of lifting weights. Like a lot of women, I thought that cardio was where it was at for so much of my life, and I would kill myself doing it, which I've never really fully enjoyed but thought that's what I needed to do, and getting my heart rate as high as I possibly could, only to not actually feel as strong or healthy in my body as I wanted to. Now that I lift weights consistently, I feel so much better. And with that comes the need to make sure we're eating enough protein. These are the things that I know really help ground me and make me feel like my best self.

SM: And has that changed during your cancer journey?

DF: Yeah, everything I just mentioned about my wellness experience has been since I discovered I had cancer, and it's not like because I wasn't doing those things that led to me getting cancer. It was more like, OK, our health is something that we take for granted when we have it. And then all of a sudden, when you find out there's something that could potentially be really detrimental, it makes you go, hmm, maybe I need to be more intentional about all of the things I'm doing, and not just throw caution to the wind and assume I'm healthy forever.

My doctor was actually the one who recommended fiber to me because as I got older I noticed that everything about the way I was going through life just felt like it got slower. My digestion got slower. So I started talking to my doctor about, like, what can I do about this feeling? I'm not regular, I feel weighed down, and my doctor said, “Are you taking any fiber?” That's when I really learned about the power of psyllium fiber. Once I added that into my day, it's been a game changer.

SM: What has surprised you the most about parenting? Or what’s been, so far, the most shocking thing you didn’t expect?

DF: The most shocking thing that I don't think anybody can prepare you for when you have kids is the amount of self-parenting you have to do while raising them. Your flaws come to the surface so fast when you see them emulating you, and you go, Well, where did you get that? And then you're like, Oh. Right. I think it's from me. So adjusting the way I talk to myself, adjusting the way I carry myself.

My oldest son has very much internalized my perfectionism, which has been very difficult for me, because it's painful to watch someone be so hard on themselves when it's just unnecessary. On the one hand, it's painful because I want to stop him from having that mindset and from being so hard on himself. And on the other hand, it's really beautiful because it's forced me to be nicer to myself. I am much easier to make a mistake and think, if I react to this mistake... he's going to think that's an appropriate response to what just happened. And, Danielle, it's not. It's OK. So he, in a lot of ways, is helping me be kinder to myself because I want him to emulate that and not emulate being hard on himself.

SM: Switching gears a little bit, you grew up on camera in a show about growing up. How has that shaped how you've parented, if at all?

DF: I think the thing it has shaped is knowing that the bite-sized 22-minute lessons we get on TV, while absolutely beneficial — and there are things I look at Alan and Amy Matthews and I think, Man, if I could strive to be like them in this way, I would want to do that — life isn't always wrapped up with a pretty bow at the end of 22 minutes.

I try to remind myself that hardships or issues you have in either your marriage or as a parent or with your children, they're all normal. No one goes through life completely unscathed, and even if our social media feeds make it look like everyone's got it all figured out and all got it together, my neighbors are both probably dealing with exactly the same things or, if not the same thing, something very similar in their own lives to what I'm going through, and it's all part of the process.

SM: Speaking of growing up, we both grew up during toxic body culture. What was that like navigating that as someone in the public eye?

DF: I'm so thankful that we didn't have social media, because even though I was in the public eye, I didn't necessarily have to deal with what people were saying about me, because there was no real way for me to know what people were saying about me. But I still had to deal with the general imagery of what was being held up as the epitome of beauty standards. Back in the day, it was like heroin chic, just absolute waifs, all those words floating around. And I was never that body type, you know? It's always difficult when whatever society decides is the beauty standard du jour, and you don't fit it. You definitely feel like you are on the outside.

With that said, I think it's almost impossible to go through your teenage years not feeling like an outsider about something. So, although the body image stuff was very difficult in the '90s, I wasn't the only one who went through that either. You could just be in high school and not on TV and not feel like you were fitting what society was calling beautiful. I think I'm just one of any other girl from that generation who didn't fit that stereotype and we all felt the same way.

SM: I will personally say that I have boobs, and I remember seeing you on TV, and I was like, she looks like me. And I was very happy that I saw someone who looked a little bit like me. Although you had fabulous eyes and fabulous hair, but it made me feel better. So thank you for that.

DF: I appreciate that because yes, that was something I remember as a teen feeling like, like, how come shirts don't fit me the same way? How come when you can wear a button-down shirt, and all the buttons lay nicely? And when I put on a button-up shirt, I either have to wear a huge oversized button-up or one where it's pulling everywhere.

SM: Have you talked to your kids about that at all? Or are they too young?

DF: They are still pretty young, but we have definitely talked about the idea that we don't comment on people's bodies. I do think that's important for them to understand because I don't want there to be certain words that are necessarily worse than others. And I don't want them to feel like they can't describe somebody or themselves in whichever way they want to. But commenting on something that, for the most part, is out of people's control, and thinking about bodies in any other way other than they are all different, and they are all fine, they're all acceptable, they're all beautiful. They're all something to think of what our bodies are capable of doing. And so, that's kind of been my thing, is like, we don't talk about other people's bodies. We just don't.

SM: Have your kids watched Boy Meets World or Girl Meets World yet?

DF: My oldest son wanted to see an episode of Boy Meets World a few years ago; I think he was maybe 3 or 4 at the time. So I played Season 1, Episode 4, which was my first episode on the show, and I'm thinking, Oh my gosh, this is such a big moment. He's gonna love this! And I come on screen and I go, “That's mommy!” And he looks at me, and he looks at the TV, and he's watching for a few minutes, and I'm looking at him going, Oh my gosh, this is so special. And he looks over at me, he goes, “OK, I'm bored, let’s watch something else.” And I went, “OK, you’re not ready for this yet. No problem.” So I'm gonna wait. I think maybe 9 or 10 is kind of the perfect time to start the show in Season 1, and then my goal will be to binge-watch it the whole way through.

SM: Switching gears, who are you rooting for on Dancing with the Stars?

DF: I mean, first of all, I'm completely blown away by the season already. There is no way around it for me: I am 100% all in on Pasha [Pashkov] and Amber [Glenn]. I am so excited for Pasha to have a partner like her who has such incredible athleticism. I'm so excited for them and I'm really rooting for them. With that said, I'm also really rooting for Tatyana Ali. How could I not? She's a friend of mine. We go all the way back to the ‘90s. I'm also very excited about Julia Stiles. There are so many good people to root for. I am absolutely about women power! I am, like, all in on all of the women.

SM: Do you sit and watch them dance or do you have to move around?

DF: I sit and watch it, but then every time, through the results, I stand up and I pace. There is no way you can have lived through standing up there as part of one of those bottom three, just even seeing the red lights, I just got chills thinking about it. It is not a good feeling. I know how hard everyone is working. And so even if you can say, well, being that someone had to go home this week, yes, that was the “right” person to go home. You still know how devastating it is. So that's the only part I can't relax through.

SM: OK, so tell me what you have coming up next. I know you have a book coming out and so much good stuff happening.

DF: Yeah, so we have a book coming out that we're really excited about, Book Meets World. I also have “Dugout Dads,” which I did with Patrick Renna from The Sandlot. We did a YouTube show and all nine episodes are available now. They're short-form, but they're still horizontal. And we're taking that out to pitch. We're using it as a great proof of concept, and we're taking it to networks, and we're taking it to streamers, and we hope to get full 22-minute episodes out of that. No matter what, there will be a whole season.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#129. Disney+ Has Adapted Your Favorite 'Goosebumps' Books — But Which Ones?

The new Disney+ Goosebumps has 10 episodes in this series, all with links to the original R.L. Stine books.

For over 30 years, Goosebumps books have scared children silly. A gateway for children to step into the world of horror novels, this R.L. Stine mega-franchise has maintained its spot as one of the best-selling book series of all time. These books combined just the right amount of kid-friendly spookiness with a dash of humor, complete with twist endings that always left readers demanding more.

Goosebumps is no stranger to screen adaptations, including a four-season live-action series on Fox Kids in the mid-90s, and a pair of movies with Jack Black from a few years ago. This Halloween season, Goosebumps is back with an all-new live-action show streaming on Disney+ and Hulu, promising more mature frights while remaining faithful to the original material. This series follows five small-town high-school kids investigating the death of a teen from three decades prior, whose home the new English teacher has just moved into.

As opposed to its 90’s counterpart, this modern adaptation will be a spine-tingling 10-part mini-series, with the first five chapters dropping on October 13, and subsequent episodes added weekly. Instead of transforming a single book into a self-contained 30-minute mini-movie, the new series takes inspiration from them, inserting those elements into the overarching narrative across the duration of the show.

According to an official press release from Scholastic, the show draws elements from five of the books, but the recently revealed titles for the episodes show nearly all of them evoke fan favorites from across the 62 original books, with links across the entire 230+ books in this expansive franchise.

Which Goosebumps books can viewers expect to see in the new show? Readers beware – you’re in for a scare!

Official trailer for Goosebumps on Disney+ and Hulu

Throughout the trailer, we see Miles McKenna as James and Zack Morris as Isaiah causing trouble with a Polaroid camera. The story that develops is taken from the fourth Goosebumps book, which shares the same name as the episode (a trend throughout most of these titles).

A group of friends discover a cursed camera in a rundown house, but instead of snapping a pic of the moment, it predicts a grim future for whoever is photographed. Scary movies and cameras are always a bad mix, no matter if it’s for photos or videos. It’s also a reminder – never take things you find in decrepit abandoned houses, unless you want to be a character in an R.L. Stine book, and you know how they tend to end up.

Seen briefly in the trailer is a lifelike human face attached to a slab of wood. It’s a mask, but just any kind. It’s a recurring haunted object seen throughout the Goosebumps franchise. These self-aware parasitic masks were created by a mysterious shopkeeper, hungry to be worn so they can completely take over the body of the wearer.

“The Haunted Mask” was the 11th book in the series and is among the most popular for adaptations into different media. In addition to being one of the few books to have a direct sequel (“The Haunted Mask II”), the masks made an appearance in the recent live-action movies, were an item found in the 2015 video game, and returned to the books over a decade later in “The Scream of the Haunted Mask.”

What tied them all together was Carly Beth Caldwell, the child who defeated them in the first entry of the saga back in 1993. Don’t be shocked if that name comes up once again in this new show!

Cuckoo clocks are a classic trope in horror, loud pendulous machinery that lulls the audience into a false sense of security, right on time for a jump scare leaping out of the furniture. In the 28th Goosebumps book, “The Cuckoo Clock of Doom,” flipped that cliché is flipped on its head by instead becoming a sinister time-travel device that could go years into the past, and even undo the existence of people.

In the trailer for the new series, James and Isiah were seen playing with the cursed camera, but the repercussions of that might not have been revealed. The following scene shows a cluster of those two characters in a cave, meaning those two might be involved in some time-altering dilemmas thanks to the clock.

Ana Yi Puig as Isabella from “The Cuckoo Clock of Doom”

The 21st Goosebumps book was a play on the 1973 classic kids’ book by Thomas Rockwell, “How to Eat Fried Worms.” The exception was that the main character in Stine’s version wasn’t paid $50 to devour the wriggling bugs, and instead “supernaturally” found their way into clothing and food.

While the true cause of this ruckus wasn’t actually revenge-seeking worms, the book ended with an enormous worm erupting from the ground, one of the more surreal third acts in the franchise. The trailer doesn’t show much in the way of insects, but get ready for some potential gross-outs if the show follows any scenes from the book, unless you don’t mind finding a half-bitten worm in your sandwich.

The fifth and seventh episodes of the new series aren’t named after a specific edition, but an entire sub-series in the Goosebumps literary universe. “Reader Beware” – besides being what R.L. Stine used to introduce some of the live-action ’90s shows – was the tagline for the “Give Yourself Goosebumps” imprint.

Totaling 50 volumes, these were interactive books that offered readers multiple ways to control the outcome of events. Imagine “Choose Your Own Adventure” books, but with titles like “Welcome to the Wicked Wax Museum,” “Escape from Camp Run-For-Your-Life,” and “Secret Agent Grandma.” A screenshot from this episode shows the kids enraptured with glossy, darkened eyes while listening to a mysterious figure read from a mysterious tome, so perhaps the teens will unwittingly be pulling the strings of some events unknown to them. Speaking of strings...

There can’t be anything made under the slimy Goosebumps umbrella without Slappy the Dummy making an appearance!

The sixth and ninth episodes of the 2023 TV series share titles, with the latter being Part 2 of this story. All of the “Night of the Living Dummy” books star Slappy, the de facto face of the Goosebumps franchise. He debuted in the seventh book of the series in 1993, and returned multiple times over the years to torment more hapless children, including the movies and the 90s TV series. Slappy was so popular that this malevolent ventriloquist’s dummy even had his own series of books, “SlappyWorld.”

Puppets can often be a scary thing for kids, and Stine admitted in his autobiography that this character originated from his own aversion to puppets, specifically Pinocchio. He later took back control of that fear by using his own dummy to scare his brother, a formative moment for Stine en route to writing horror books.

The 15th book in the original series, “You Can’t Scare Me” has one of my favorite Tim Jacobus covers, giving readers a sneak peek at the terrors lurking inside its pages. This one features the Mud Monsters, reanimated corpses of town residents from yesteryear who drowned in a flood in Greene Forest, and rise up once a year to seek revenge on those who refused to help.

There are no murky dirt zombies to be found in the trailer, so this one may be in name only, but I wouldn’t be disappointed if I saw these turbid golems rampaging in the woods once during the series.

The cast of high-school kids entranced in something sinister from the episode “Give Yourself Goosebumps”

The finale for the 2023 series brings us to another mainstay in the Goosebumps universe, HorrorLand!

This ghoulish theme park debuted in the sixteenth book in the series back in 1994 and is another popular part of the franchise. Run by the HorrorLand Horrors, sadistic monsters who can only be defeated by pinching them, this is far from the happiest place on earth. Their motto is “Where Nightmares Come to Life!” and features rides like The Coffin Cruise, Ferris Squeal, and Wheel of Misfortune.

Besides a direct sequel, this volume has been adapted over the years into a board game, comics, three different video games, a two-part episode in the 90’s show, and spun off into its own series that concluded by bringing notable characters from past books together to take on this haunted establishment. This marked the first serialized tale in Stine’s Goosebumps franchise, a fitting title to close out this new series, which also follows a single narrative amidst the disparate scary events these five high-schoolers contend with.

Earlier this May, a different R.L. Stine series, Just Beyond, was pulled from Disney+ along with many other shows and films during a period when many streaming platforms were culling their content. It seems like Disney is hedging their bets on this one, with a rollout that includes the first two episodes being shown as part of Freeform’s “31 Nights of Halloween” the same night it launches online. It’s possible the new Disney+ Goosebumps could be 2023’s version of Wednesday — a scary good time of destination TV with the right amount of nostalgia, ready to scare and entertain audiences of all ages.

This article was originally published on Oct. 9, 2023

#130. I Missed My Kids’ ‘Last Halloween’

Motherhood is obsessed with firsts. Lasts get no such attention.

As a mom, there are many experiences for which people simply can’t prepare you.

I was told that contractions felt like “really bad menstrual cramps.” What contractions actually feel like? Committing hara-kiri with a knife just dull enough not to kill you but just sharp enough to make you rethink every choice that got you to that moment.

Then there’s leaving the hospital with a newborn when you’ve never so much as changed a diaper and are still wondering, So, when will her neck start working?

Of course, there are the beautiful, ineffable firsts: The first time your baby smiles at you, the first time you hear her laugh, the first steps she takes before she falls giggling into your open arms.

And the… less appetizing… firsts: The first time your kid gets lice. The first time your kid gets Hand, Foot, Mouth. The first time your kid gets pinworms. The second time your kid gets pinworms. The third time your kid gets pinworms. You get the idea.

Motherhood is obsessed with firsts. We photograph them, write them down, text them to grandparents, and post them online so people we haven’t spoken to since high school can give us a virtual thumbs up.

Nobody takes a picture of the last time you carry your child. Mostly because you don’t know it’s the last time. Also because you’re probably telling your child, “My back hurts, and you’re perfectly capable of walking!”

Nobody posts the last time your child crawls into your bed after a nightmare. Nobody texts the grandparents about the last time your child trick-or-treats with you.

Because by the time you realize any of these things have happened for the last time, it’s too late.

I grew up in New York City in a 43-story apartment building, where Halloween meant riding elevators and knocking on doors with a printed list of “participating” neighbors. It was efficient, climate-controlled, and almost completely devoid of magic.

We didn’t run down tree-lined streets in packs, ringing doorbells, leaves crunching under our feet like the kids in the movies. That was pure Hollywood fantasy to me. I thought I wanted E.T. Halloween. Apparently, I just wanted suburbs.

So, when my husband and I got pregnant with our first child, we moved to a house in Hancock Park in Los Angeles. Not exactly the suburbs — but for a born-and-bred city girl, close enough.

We brought our daughter home from the hospital on October 31, 2009, at the height of the swine flu epidemic. Doctors — and grandparents — warned us about germy kids around a newborn, so we turned off our porch light and taped a sign to the door: “Happy Halloween! Please come back next year.”

The next Halloween, our daughter was dressed as a ladybug, too young to trick-or-treat but exactly the right age for us to take an obscene amount of photos. By 2011, she was a princess with a plastic pumpkin and a squad of toddler princess friends. I was pregnant with our second, and friends gathered at our house, parents filling roadie cups with wine and following our tiny royalty from house to house.

It was pure magic — my suburban(ish) Halloween fantasy come true.

Soon we had two kids and a new tradition: the big neighborhood photo in our front yard. Every year, more families joined. My parents flew out from New York for my daughter’s birthday and stayed for Halloween to hand out candy (though we learned the hard way that my dad should never be trusted with that much chocolate).

Every October 1, we pulled the Halloween décor bins out of the garage, bought new cobwebs and skeletons, and spent the afternoon turning the house into a haunted wonderland. Our kids loved making the house “creepy” for an entire month.

For over a decade, Halloween was my Super Bowl, the heartbeat of our family calendar — the night that defined our neighborhood, our friendships, and our kids’ childhoods.

When my husband finally retrieved the bin of decorations from the garage — a task I had been requesting since Labor Day — I opened it to find the literal (and figurative) ghosts of our Halloweens past: Costumes our kids had outgrown, headless witch décor, battery-dead mechanical spiders, a smoke machine that never worked but that we kept “just in case,” and plastic crows that had somehow lost their feet.

At two o’clock that afternoon, I started decorating the front yard.

I asked my kids to help, but my son (13) was playing video games with friends, and my daughter (16) was getting ready to go out. They were both going to parties. Neither of them would trick-or-treat that night.

My parents, now in their 80s, skipped their annual Halloween trip. Another neighbor with younger kids hosted the annual neighborhood photo. I didn’t go.

For the first time in 16 years, my husband and I were home alone on Halloween, passing out candy to other people’s kids.

I still loved seeing the costumes and the chaos and how grown-up our neighbors’ babies and kids were getting. But I’d be lying if I said it didn’t sting. The sticky hands, the plastic pumpkins, the wine-in-a-roadie walks with parent-friends — somehow that part was over for us just as we were getting the hang of it.

I realized that I’d somehow missed our “last Halloween.”

I’ve never been one of those moms who begs time to slow down. I don’t judge those moms at all; it’s just not my vibe. I’ve loved watching my kids grow up. And I like teenagers. They sleep late. They dress themselves. They get their own snacks.

But maybe — just this one night — I wished I could rewind.

So they could be little again. So I could walk beside them in the dark. So I could hold their chocolatey hands between doorbells, run after them, pocket their wrappers and half-eaten Tootsie Rolls. So I could pick them up and carry them when they got scared or tired, and feel their soft arms tight around my neck.

Sixteen years earlier, we turned off the porch light because we had just brought our newborn daughter home from the hospital. She was tiny and helpless, and our job was to keep her safe.

Now she was 16 and at a Halloween party with her friends. Keeping her safe meant something entirely different. It meant letting her go, trusting her to make good choices, and hoping we’d given her enough to find her way home.

As I reached for the porch light switch, my phone buzzed with a text from my daughter.

I love you, Mom. I will always be trick or treating with you in my heart.

I left the light on. I knew she would turn it off when she got home. And I’d be waiting up until she did.

Jordan Roter is a screenwriter, TV writer, producer and author of the novel MOMS LIKE US. She lives in Los Angeles with her husband, kids, and their dog, Alfie.

#131. One Controversial 'Bluey' Character Isn’t Actually All That Bad

There are always characters in TV shows that viewers loathe, whether it be for legitimate reasons or personal preferences. The same goes for kids’ entertainment, and that sentiment persists even in something as wholesome as Bluey. If you were to make a tiered chart of characters from this popular Australian kids' cartoon on Disney+, chances are a high percentage of fans would rank these two characters at the bottom – Muffin and Judo. We’ll save the Heelers’ Chow Chow neighbor for another day, but Bluey’s cousin Muffin is a divisive one among its audience.

Muffin’s fiery temper has landed her in some hilarious situations, but it’s also made Bluey fans leery of her. Brash, spoiled, and tantrum-prone, many have compared this member of the extended Heeler family to Angelica Pickles from The Rugrats. It’s easy to take Muffin at face value as a prima donna, but she’s another case of Bluey showing kids and parents in a more realistic light.

Despite her behavior, Muffin is the prime example that no child is irredeemable, holding an uncomfortable mirror up to expose some unpleasant truths about raising kids, and certainly worth a deeper look at why she’s really one of the best in the show.

Muffin’s debut in “BBQ” proves what happens when the immovable object meets the irresistable force

Even from her first appearance in season one’s “BBQ,” Muffin was a chaotic force of nature. She’s like a wild pony, unable to be tamed no matter how hard anyone tried unless she took the reins for her own sake. There are plenty of examples of Muffin’s bratty tendencies across the series, making it understandable why this kid has such a rough time getting fan support.

She was mildly antagonistic to her older cousin in “Horsey Ride,” being a know-it-all when her younger sister Socks was nomming on Bluey’s special toy. Season two showed us how demanding Muffin could be in “Charades” and “Library,” and she was just plain bonkers in “Sleepover,” but there’s no culprit to blame on that other than lack of sleep.

No shortage of episodes display the negative traits of this character, but many show her as a precocious child who just likes to have fun. Muffin was following Bluey’s play pattern when it came time to defend their nail salon in “Stumpfest”, the same as she did in “Backpackers.” She’s also genuinely well-mannered in the Christmas episodes, unrelated to Santa visiting their home, and has been a good big sister with her sibling, even helping the pup hold an ice pop in “Charades.” Even in season three’s “Pizza Girls,” Muffin was more about anarchy than she was about disobedience and stirring up trouble.

Chaos, thy name is Muffin Heeler! Still from season three’s “Faceytalk”

Muffin’s turning point occurs in season three’s “Faceytalk,” which is about the Heeler children virtually playing together on tablets. The episode begins with Bluey’s mum, Chilli, reminding Bluey not to hog the screen from Bingo, “because we know what happens when you hog.” While this may seem like a simple lesson, it falls into the deeper message of the episode as the plot progresses.

Muffin wants to finish drawing a hat on the Faceytalk screen before turning the tablet over to her little sister, Socks, and resists the boundary Stripe places on her screen time. Trixie, meanwhile, has washed her hands of the situation because she has “somewhere to be.” Remember, Muffin is around four years old here and is testing the limits of what she can and can’t do. There’s no intent of malice on her part since, in her mind, all Muffin wants is to doodle her pink cowboy hat. Stripe gets in the way of her finishing that task, but has difficulty being firm and following through with what he says. After Muffin absconds with Stripe’s phone, a wild chase through the house forces Trixie’s involvement and leads to a standoff with her husband instead of her unruly daughter.

“Faceytalk” isn’t just about Muffin’s problems with sharing, because the root of the problem starts with her parents. From the onset, the couple had communication problems regarding how to handle their kids and being on the same page with each other. In the last act of this episode, it all comes crashing down into the event that permanently changes who Muffin becomes.

The running theme through this story was “hogging” things, and Stripe felt like Trixie hogged the kids when it came to discipline, and undermined him, while Trixie felt Stripe wasn’t doing things the way she wanted and was therefore inferior to her decisions. In the end, the pair find unity in their parenting, and in doing so, start a cascade effect on Muffin that begins to see the character make some changes of her own.

This granny is about to find out what happens when you mess with Muffin

A few episodes later, “Granny Mobile” brings us the threequel to the Granny series. This story marked the first time Muffin appeared since “Faceytalk,” and the difference in her personality is immediately noticeable.

The Heelers, with Muffin joining them for a playdate, visit their neighbor Doreen’s yard sale. After seeing a mobility scooter for sale, the girls decide to play Grannies, with Muffin playing the part of Gladys the “grouchy granny.” After spending some time as this character, Muffin tells Bluey she isn’t enjoying being so mean but is unsure how to play the part differently.

As Doreen struggles to not be such a pushover during her yard sale, a real grouchy granny shows up demanding to buy the scooter for a fraction of its actual price. Muffin, so lost in her elderly persona that Daniel Day-Lewis would be impressed, grouches back to the actual octogenarian, and uses her Muffin powers for good instead of evil, helping Doreen get four times the asking price for the vehicle.

Muffin’s good deeds showed her there was a time and place for her authoritative voice, acting as positive reinforcement that it’s possible to still follow the boundaries set by her parents while also maintaining her inner self. If anything, this proved Muffin can stand up for others the same way she used to for herself, advocating for the voiceless in whatever situation may occur. How this realization will be used in future stories remains to be seen, but the evolution of Muffin is clear now, and the road ahead is starting to look much less bumpy than her wild ride in “Sleepover.”

Muffin might be pure unbridled chaos, but we wouldn’t have her any other way

It’s important to remember that Muffin is only around four years old by the end of season three, so her emotional development is still in flux as she learns about boundaries. If her behavior was like this as an adult, it would certainly be a call for alarm, but this is relatively normal for a preschooler.

Outgrowing this phase will naturally happen through her mum and dad collaboratively parenting their child, and supporting each other. It won’t be easy and there will likely be more disagreements as they figure things out, but seeing how quickly Muffin changed in season three, it proved it’s never too late to make positive changes that will enhance the attitude of their kid while improving communication with each other.

While some parents may fear their children reenacting the negative traits of Muffin, or others may label her “annoying,” watching someone like Muffin grow onscreen is vital for kids and adults to observe. It took some time, but Muffin is learning about the consequences of her actions while her parents strive to become better at their jobs as caregivers. If there are two things Muffin taught us, it’s that coconuts have water inside them, and it’s never too late to make a change.

#132. The World Needs An Eldest Daughter

I’m the eldest daughter of the eldest daughter, going back eight generations, and now I’m raising one. If my own family has taught me anything, it’s that this lineage could be the blueprint for something better.

My mother would have you know our lineage the minute you meet her. I am the eldest daughter of the eldest daughter of the eldest daughter, going eight times back. She is proud of it, this freakish line of vaginas slotting neatly into one another back into time and space, like Russian dolls. I always doubted her assertion that this was true, until an Ancestry.com test allowed me to access the family tree portion of the app, and I counted one, two, three, four… all the way back to eight. What could this all mean? A curse? A superpower?

The eldest daughter trope is known far and wide, mostly only to firstborn daughters. We are parentified young, destined to become the second mother. We learn to anticipate needs, predict moods; we are the latchkey to the latchkey kids. I am a people pleaser, and sure, I like to be right. Firstborn girls have a light toxicity to them. These traits make eldest daughters desperate to branch out, and I was no different. I got married young, had kids young. How much of this was by choice, how much by training?

As the eldest daughter, my boundaries are frequently trampled over, yet I am the queen of respecting boundaries. My younger brother is someone who never hides his emotions; you will know his feelings the second they emerge. I love that about him. I envy it. I am someone who holds them in, cheeks full with unspoken words I can’t seem to swallow, until the inevitable happens and I vomit them out all over you. I live at the polar caps — silently accepting or sobbing uncontrollably, depending on where in the digestion process I am.

Firstborn daughter: Is this where I am in the birth order of my family, or is this also womanhood? We are conditioned by society, our parents, and our peers to take what they give us, to hide the ugly, accentuate the good traits. Boys will be boys, we are told. He hurt you because he likes you, we are told. Beauty is pain, we are told. Perhaps the superpowers I was concerned with inheriting have nothing to do with being one in a long line of eldest daughters, but rather, a product of feminine expectation.

I don’t know much about many of my ancestors (though my debut novel explores the possibilities of ancestral hand-me-downs), but I know my grandmother, Nanny Goat, was a typical mother hen as an older sister. My mother was the same, a woman not good at clearly outlining her feelings because they hadn’t been prioritized as a child. Thanks to research and books on epigenetic trauma like Bernice McFadden’s Firstborn Girls or Dr. Joy DeGruy’s Post Traumatic Slave Syndrome, we know that the experiences of a future mother are felt, ripples across a pond, throughout generations.

Am I carrying the weight of my foremothers? Can I put it down?

My own firstborn daughter is a sweet, doe-eyed 8-year-old named Luka. Although she is growing up in a vastly different household to mine — she has doting parents who love each other, a house and a yard and a quiet community-led town to grow up in — I have noticed some eldest daughter tendencies.

She comes by these honestly; I have never made a point to give her more responsibility than appropriate, but somehow… I find her trying to feed her sister breakfast so we can sleep in. If I am unwell, she insists on being given a job to do, to help. These could be viewed as just the characteristics of a sweet, loving kid, which she is, but I worry.

I worry that the curse of the eldest daughter has found her, pure and innocent, and sought to parentify her. That is her destiny. That is who she will be, whether she (or I) like it or not. I encourage her to be selfish, to think of her own needs first. To not worry about what she looks like to others, what other people may say about her actions.

What if we invert the notion of feminine expectation? Flip the patriarchy completely, leaving capitalism’s desire for a ladder, dog-eat-dog, one-ring-to-rule-them-all behind? As we discover more about the men at the top’s penchant for corporate (and literal) cannibalism (allegedly), it is alluring.

Despite copious propaganda about the race of the sperm to the egg, it is actually the egg that chooses. It isn’t a passive victim. It is selecting, carefully. We know that DNA is favored by the maternal line. Mitochondrial DNA is passed down only from the maternal DNA, not the paternal. From NPR’s Allison Aubrey: the X chromosome contains far more genes, so that even male humans have more genes from their maternal line. The maternal line, therefore, is the one evolution is desperate to preserve.

No accident then, that my matriarchal lineage forges on. Eldest daughters, yes, but certainly not a curse.

After reading the viral Threads by author and influencer Gabrielle Blair on how patriarchy isn’t an evolutionarily sound format for society, I wondered if the repetition of eldest daughters wasn’t some meek-making trad wife factory but rather evolution's way of putting us forward as leaders. My mother is not a traditional woman. An artist and an intellectual, she has never been one to be told shit by anyone, which is another eldest daughter trait. My grandmother was quiet and Catholic, a mother of four, but she didn’t suffer fools; she was often the smartest person in the room, even if it went unnoticed.

Each seed of my ancestors that came before me brought me closer to Luka, the purest of us all. My darling Luka. An empath for sure. I asked her what she hopes for the future. She told me, “A planet where money isn’t important, where everyone has a house and food and the things they need.” I reiterated, “But Luka, what about you?” And she, with the wisdom and innocence we only ever have at 8, said, “That is about me, Mama.”

Not to place too much importance on my absolutely, positively perfect child, but isn’t that what this is about?

We need an eldest daughter. We need a matriarch-centric society. If my own family has taught me anything, it is that a lineage of eldest daughters carries the possibility of alternative futures. Our DNA is demanding it. We need empathy and leadership, and a society with the ability to see the bigger picture, to predict our needs in 10, 15, a hundred years’ time. Because the planet is changing and, hopefully, so are we.

Eirinie Carson is an award-winning Black British writer and college dropout living in California. She writes about sexual taboos, death and dying, illegal substances, hauntings both real and imagined, and ancestral inheritance in a world desperate to sever the connections between what came before and what is to come. Her first work of fiction, the maternal gothic novel Bloodfire, Baby (2026), has been named one of the year’s best debuts by Debutiful.

#133. All The Banned Or Censored Bluey Episodes — And Why They Were Given The Boot

Bluey is the most beloved show on the planet. But you can’t see all the original versions in the United States.

Bluey has become not only the biggest kids’ show on the planet but one of the most popular TV series worldwide. Period. First airing in its homeland of Australia in 2018, the realistic portrayals of parenting combined with the zany wholesome hijinks of a pair of adorable animal sisters means the show is loved equally by kids and adults.

But. Not every single moment of Bluey is available in the United States. A handful of episodes were eliminated by American censors and/or Disney. Some episodes have also been heavily censored and/or altered for American audiences. Why would a kids’ show be censored or have episodes banned? It’s a reasonable question and the easy answer is: it’s complicated. Sometimes it’s because a word has a different connotation in the U.S. than it does in Australia. Other times, there’s an innuendo, or topic U.S. censors have deemed inappropriate.

Across all seasons of Bluey, references to Australian-specific things were localized for American audiences, so we won’t spend too much time discussing those unless they were explicitly censored for serious implications (as serious as Bluey can be, anyway). Likewise, certain bits of dialogue were altered through the series for various reasons, and unless it was something provocative, this article will also glance past those changes.

So, without further ado, here’s a full list of censored and banned Bluey episodes as of May 2023, including one very recent body-shaming moment in Australia.

Update! This list now includes 2024 Disney+ versions of Season 3 episodes!

The good info about the first season is currently no episodes are banned in the U.S. anymore. However, a few notable changes were made to them, some of which were censored and altered outside of Australia.

What was censored and why? A fairly wholesome and hilarious episode, this episode and two others from the first season, “Shaun” and “Teasing,” along with “Flat Pack” from Season 2 were censored due to the use of a racially-insensitive term that could refer to Aboriginal people. The ABC apologized and claimed it was not intended to refer to that abhorrent use of that word. “Daddy Robot” and the other episodes now use a nonsense word to replace the derogatory phrase.

Update: “Teasing” was restored on Disney+ when Bluey season 3B was added, replacing the offensive phrase with “Shoobi-doo-wop”.

What was censored and why? A scene where Bluey is playing “Penguins” in the bathroom was cut from the U.K. and the U.S., although it’s still referenced in the episode. The cut scene has Bluey sliding around the room, something that could be dangerous for a kid to do on a wet tiled floor.

What was it censored and why? The episode ends in the U.S. with Bandit finally boarding his imaginary airplane, only to realize the reckless cab driver is also his pilot. However, the original version continues after that realization, with Bingo’s character pretending to throw up on Bandit’s lap. In the U.S. version, there is no vomit, and that’s why the episode ends earlier here than in the original one.

What was censored and why? As the girls are looking for a way to use some cash, they meet a unicorn handler (actually a pony with a horn on her head). Bluey is excited at this idea but learns only one of them can have a ride on her. Their disappointment quickly disappears after the unicorn drops a huge turd on the grass, leaving the kids fleeing as they scream their heads off. The turd does not exist in the Disney+ version.

This horse and her owner were seen again in the Season 3 episode “Pass the Parcel,” only this time the horse had already relieved itself. In the original version, her feces can be seen in a wide shot where the kids are playing the game, but the American version has an alternate version with the poo pile missing.

What was censored and why? At one point in the episode, Bingo asks her dad how babies get into mom’s bellies. This line is cut in the U.S. version. Apparently, Disney doesn’t want pregnancy discussed in-depth in a show aimed at preschoolers.

The second season brought a few new challenges to the show that needed resolutions, including one episode that will probably remain in the Disney vault until the end of time.

Why was it banned? Similar to “Daddy Putdown,” this one is even more focused on pregnancy and carrying babies. The episode does not exist on Disney+ and in the U.S. at all. In it, Bandit (the dad) simulates what it’s like to give birth. The entire episode is banned as a result.

Will it be unbanned? Most likely never. Unlike “Family Meeting” (aka “the fart episode”) it appears this one is not coming to Disney+ anytime soon.

Why was it changed? Jack seems to act like a child with ADHD. Although he is too young to comprehend the way his brain understands the world around him, he knows it works differently from others.

In the original version, Jack tells Rusty “There’s something wrong with me.” It was later revised to “There’s something going on with me.”

Why was it censored? Bluey hands Conductor Bandit something when he asks for her ticket that she instructs him to rub all over his face. In the original version, imaginary poop was passed to her dad. In America, the line was changed to transform that invisible heap into a slug.

Why was it censored? We already discussed earlier how this one was hit with the same racially-insensitive insult heard in “Daddy Robot,” but there may be another reason this one was controversial.

The core of this episode is a whirlwind examination of the cycle of life, rife with metaphors and silliness to keep it light. However, this episode does include a part that can be interpreted as an afterlife, and it’s also possible to see this plot as a baby’s first look at evolution.

Currently, the episode is available on all platforms in the U.S. with only the derogatory term removed. If you haven’t seen it in a while, it’s a deeply moving six minutes worthy of a rewatch.

The release of this season has been split into several batches of episodes. At the time of publication, Australia is about to get the third part of the season, with no plans on when it will come to the United States.

What was censored? The episode opens with Bandit looking unhappy about the results of weighing himself, grabbing his sides remorsefully. Chilli shows similar dissatisfaction when she does the same. Arguably one of the biggest chunks to be edited out of this show, “Exercise” turned into a huge divisive battle immediately with accusations of fat-shaming, and concerns centered around body dysmorphia in children and adults. Ultimately, the first minute of this episode was removed across all global distributors due to these concerns, instead starting in the backyard with Bandit beginning his workout routine and no discussion on the shape of his body. To be clear, this episode has not even aired yet in the US.

Why was it censored? In one flashback, Bandit is playing “Boomerang” with Bluey while having a conversation with Fido. In the original version, the conversation seems to be about getting neutered, or in human terms having a vasectomy. When it arrived in the U.S., it was changed to be about having Bandit’s dog teeth removed.

Why was it censored? In a scene where Bingo and Bluey teach Bandit how to use a swing, the girls intentionally position him so it hits him in the crotch, causing him to cry out, “My groin!” That word is eliminated in the U.S. version.

Also in S3, the word “groin” is edited out of the U.S. version of “Chores” when Bandit complains about hurting his groin after attempting to do Bingo’s “Bee-yoop” silly walk.

Why was it censored? When Bingo proves to Bluey she’s annoying too, only in a different way, the younger sister tapes her nose back and puts fake teeth into her mouth. Bluey says she looks “crazy” in the Australian version. The word “crazy” does not appear in the U.S. version.

As opposed to an abrupt cut to hide something like Bandit’s groin hit in “Born Yesterday,” the cut is not noticeable at all and adds to the element of surprise once Bingo reveals herself.

Why was it censored? While having an imaginary drive with Bluey that starts to take a turn into madness, her stuffed cat Agatha threatens to pee on the curtains. In the censored version, Agatha instead tells them she’ll scratch their curtains.

What was censored? When Muffin goes on a rampage and tries to escape from her dad while still on the call, she runs around the house, eventually smashing into the bathroom, which Trixie is using. In the original version, Trixie can be clearly seen on the toilet, forced to cover herself up. The American edit crops this out, instead keeps the shot tight on Muffin’s face so as not to reveal the scene behind her.

Update: As of the summer of 2023, “Faceytalk” has been restored to the original version, with Trixie easily seen seated in the bathroom.

Why was it censored? Unicorse is using his best moves to get on Chilli’s good side in the worst way possible. While showing off his sweet moves, Chilli remarks about the chili sauce stain on his body. Australians heard Unicorse respond with, “Wanna’ lick?” The American version has altered this to “Want a bit?”

Why was it censored? Twice in “The Decider,” the two families of sports fans tease each other by saying their team will “flog” the opponents. A term more commonly used with Australian sports fans than Americans, Disney+ viewers will instead hear “beat” due to the violent implications of what the other word means.

Why was it banned? The obvious reason is the sheer volume of references to passing gas. There isn’t any real potty humor here, but the impetus of the episode is based around a silent but deadly affront to poor Bluey’s nose.

Why was it banned? In the opening moments of "Relax," Bandit calls the kids "Super Troopers" in the US edit. However, in the original Australian version, he refers to his girls as "Dingle Berries." What's so controversial about a nonsense word? Turns out the phrase has more than one meaning, and while many know it as a way to insult someone's intelligence, it stems from something more fecal. Apparently, when it comes to Disney Plus, bathroom humor and Bluey mix like cereal and windshield washer fluid, so those berries were better left where they belonged.

If you’re looking to find all the episodes closer to how they looked when they initially aired, the only way is to get the DVD of Season 1 and Season 2, which is region-specific to the United States. There are also other ways to find Bluey episodes, but even the hardiest of Pomeranians wouldn’t dare look in those dark corners of the web. Occasionally, the ban does lift on an episode, but so far, that’s only happened once or twice.

Non-banned Bluey episodes air on Disney+ in the United States.

This article was originally published on March 27, 2023

#134. Sensual Scalp Massage Is The New Foreplay, According To Sex Experts

Adding some 10-minute head rubs here and there can also increase your connection outside the bedroom.

The world feels more divided than perhaps it ever has, but I think we can all still agree on one simple truth: It feels really freaking good when someone plays with your hair. The best part of the haircut is that scalp massage at the bowl. Your partner idly combing their fingers through your hair while you watch a movie — hnnnnng. So maybe it comes as no surprise that your scalp can actually be considered an erogenous zone, according to sex experts. So, if you know your partner loves a good head rub, here’s how you can work that into your intimate arsenal.

According to the International Society for Sexual Medicine, an erogenous zone is “any part of the body that elicits sexual arousal when touched.” Of course, most of us immediately think of the usual erogenous zones, but anywhere that a gentle graze, scratch, kiss, or bite gets your engine revving also counts. Because the scalp is so densely populated with nerve endings (like those other body parts your mind first jumped to), yes, a scalp massage can easily become quite the turn-on.

For the record, this doesn’t mean every scalp scratch has to be sexual; it’s just a new area of the body with untapped potential. And when you’re in a long-term relationship, it’s nice to be reminded of these low-lift but fresh new ways to turn each other on.

“A typical scalp massage is usually associated with relaxation, while a sensual massage is slower and more deliberate. You’re paying attention not just to what you’re doing, but also to how your partner is responding to it. And sensual doesn’t necessarily mean sexual. Sometimes we forget there’s a whole world of touch between ‘friendly’ and ‘let’s have sex,’” says Angie Rowntree, ABS, board-certified sexologist and founder and filmmaker behind the award-winning ethical adult film site Sssh.com.

Well there’s the obvious: They feel fantastic. Scalp massages can be a form of foreplay, or a way to show your partner some love.

“There’s something very intimate about having someone play with your hair or massage your scalp. It’s nurturing, it’s pleasurable, and it asks absolutely nothing of you except to enjoy it. I think that may be part of why people are so drawn to it. We’re constantly stimulated, but that doesn’t necessarily mean we’re connected,” Rowntree says. “We’re on our phones, answering emails, scrolling, watching TV while scrolling some more, and then someone gives you 10 minutes of their complete attention? That feels different.”

A lil’ head rub can also be a great way to add more touch that doesn’t lead to sex into your relationship. Making space for intimacy outside the bedroom fuels your connection.

“I think people are becoming much more comfortable with the idea that pleasure doesn’t always have to be about sex or orgasm. Sometimes pleasure is having someone run their fingers through your hair while you lie there and do absolutely nothing,” she adds.

Here’s how to give one of those hair salon-quality, groan-inducing scalp massages, according to Rowntree:

Finally, offer scalp massages (or request them) outside of trying to initiate sex. “When people don’t feel as though there’s an expectation attached to the touch, they’re often able to relax and enjoy all the sensations. And, of course, sometimes relaxing into it leads somewhere else,” says Rowntree.
